concepts.title: The Cell
concepts.subtitle: The smallest living unit
concepts.simple: Your brain is made of tiny living units called cells. Each cell is like a miniature workplace with a boundary, energy supply and instructions.
concepts.psych: Neural tissue is cellular. Neurons and glia share core organelles, but specialise for signalling, support, defence and myelination.
concepts.advanced: The plasma membrane establishes electrochemical separation. The nucleus regulates gene expression; mitochondria generate ATP; ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum synthesise proteins required for receptors, channels and structural maintenance.
concepts.analogy: A self-contained clinic: walls control entry, the records room stores instructions, and the generator powers every service.
concepts.care: Cellular energy failure, membrane instability and impaired protein handling can alter cognition, mood and behaviour before gross structural changes are visible.
concepts.wrong: Hypoxia, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation and toxic exposure can disrupt cellular metabolism and communication.
concepts.pearl: Psychological function depends on biological systems that are active, adaptive and metabolically expensive.

quiz.question: Which structure primarily controls what enters and leaves a cell?
options: Plasma membrane
Nucleus
Mitochondrion
Ribosome
quiz.explanation: The plasma membrane selectively regulates movement between the cell and its environment.

concepts.title: The Cell Membrane
concepts.subtitle: A selective electrical boundary
concepts.simple: The membrane is the cell’s flexible skin. It decides what can pass and helps keep the inside electrically different from the outside.
concepts.psych: Ion gradients across the membrane make neural signalling possible. Channels, pumps and receptors translate chemical and electrical events into cellular responses.
concepts.advanced: The phospholipid bilayer is selectively permeable. Na+/K+-ATPase maintains sodium and potassium gradients, while ligand-gated and voltage-gated channels alter membrane conductance and excitability.
concepts.analogy: A secure border with gates, scanners and staff who use energy to keep traffic moving in the correct direction.
concepts.care: Many psychoactive medications act at membrane receptors, transporters or ion channels rather than changing brain structure directly.
concepts.wrong: Channelopathies, toxins and electrolyte disturbance can produce seizures, confusion, weakness or altered arousal.
concepts.pearl: A neuron’s “decision” to fire emerges from thousands of membrane events summing over time and space.

quiz.question: What maintains the major sodium and potassium gradients?
options: Na+/K+-ATPase
DNA polymerase
Myelin
Microtubules
quiz.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to preserve the gradients that support resting potential and action potentials.

concepts.title: Brain Electricity
concepts.subtitle: Voltage created by ions
concepts.simple: Brain electricity is not like a wire in a wall. It comes from charged particles moving through tiny gates in cell membranes.
concepts.psych: Membrane voltage reflects unequal ion distribution. Excitatory and inhibitory inputs shift the probability that a neuron will generate an action potential.
concepts.advanced: Resting potential is dominated by potassium leak conductance and maintained gradients. Depolarisation toward threshold recruits voltage-gated sodium channels; repolarisation follows sodium inactivation and potassium efflux.
concepts.analogy: A stadium wave: each person moves locally, but the organised pattern travels across the crowd.
concepts.care: EEG reflects summed postsynaptic activity from synchronised cortical populations, not single-neuron action potentials.
concepts.wrong: Excess excitation, reduced inhibition or disturbed ion balance can destabilise networks and increase seizure risk.
concepts.pearl: Electrical activity is the medium; information is carried by timing, pattern, location and network context.

quiz.question: EEG primarily reflects which activity?
options: Summed postsynaptic potentials
Individual axon action potentials
Blood glucose
Skull vibration
quiz.explanation: Scalp EEG mainly captures synchronised postsynaptic currents generated by large cortical populations.

concepts.title: Brain Chemistry
concepts.subtitle: Messages across microscopic gaps
concepts.simple: Neurons often pass messages by releasing chemicals into a tiny gap. The next cell reads the chemical with matching receptors.
concepts.psych: Neurotransmission depends on synthesis, vesicular release, receptor binding and signal termination through reuptake, diffusion or enzymatic breakdown.
concepts.advanced: Calcium influx at the presynaptic terminal triggers SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion. Postsynaptic effects vary by receptor subtype, intracellular signalling and the receiving cell’s current state.
concepts.analogy: A keycard system: the same messenger can open one door, lock another, or do nothing when the reader is absent.
concepts.care: “Chemical imbalance” is an inadequate clinical model. Symptoms arise from dynamic circuits, learning, physiology and context—not a single low or high transmitter.
concepts.wrong: Receptor dysregulation, impaired clearance, medication interactions and substance use can alter signalling across multiple networks.
concepts.pearl: A neurotransmitter has no fixed psychological meaning outside its receptor, circuit, timing and context.

quiz.question: What directly triggers vesicle release at the presynaptic terminal?
options: Calcium influx
Chloride efflux
Myelin formation
Gene transcription
quiz.explanation: Incoming action potentials open voltage-gated calcium channels, initiating vesicle fusion and transmitter release.

concepts.title: Meet the Brain
concepts.subtitle: One organ, many coordinated systems
concepts.simple: The brain is a team of regions that share information. No single area works completely alone.
concepts.psych: Functions emerge from distributed networks spanning cortex, subcortex, cerebellum and brainstem. Regional specialisation matters, but connectivity determines performance.
concepts.advanced: Large-scale networks dynamically reconfigure according to task demands, arousal and learning. Structure–function relationships are probabilistic, not one-to-one mappings.
concepts.analogy: An orchestra: sections specialise, but the music depends on timing, coordination and the conductor’s changing demands.
concepts.care: Avoid reverse inference—observing activation in a region does not prove a specific thought, diagnosis or emotion.
concepts.wrong: Focal lesions can disrupt specialised functions, while diffuse or connectivity disturbances may produce broader cognitive and emotional effects.
concepts.pearl: Think in systems first, regions second, and isolated “brain centres” last.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects modern neuroscience?
options: Functions emerge from distributed networks
Each emotion has one brain centre
The cortex works independently
Connectivity is clinically irrelevant
quiz.explanation: Most psychological functions rely on coordinated activity across distributed, interacting networks.

concepts.title: The Cerebral Lobes
concepts.subtitle: Useful landmarks, not sealed compartments
concepts.simple: The cortex is divided into lobes that help us describe where things happen. The borders are landmarks, not walls.
concepts.psych: Frontal systems support executive control and action; parietal systems integrate sensory-spatial information; temporal systems support audition, memory and meaning; occipital cortex processes vision.
concepts.advanced: Each lobe contains multiple cytoarchitectonic and functional areas with extensive intra- and inter-lobar connectivity. Clinical effects depend on lesion side, extent, network position and premorbid organisation.
concepts.analogy: Suburbs in one city: each has a recognisable character, but roads and services cross every boundary.
concepts.care: Lobe-based summaries are useful for formulation but too coarse for definitive localisation or diagnosis.
concepts.wrong: Injury may produce executive dysfunction, neglect, aphasia, agnosia or visual field deficits depending on network involvement.
concepts.pearl: Use lobes to orient yourself; use networks and behaviour to reason clinically.

quiz.question: Which lobe is most directly associated with primary visual processing?
options: Occipital
Frontal
Temporal
Parietal
quiz.explanation: Primary visual cortex is located in the occipital lobe.

concepts.title: Below the Cortex
concepts.subtitle: Subcortical systems shape the whole brain
concepts.simple: Important structures sit deep inside the brain. They help control movement, memory, emotion, motivation and body regulation.
concepts.psych: The thalamus coordinates information flow; basal ganglia support action selection and habit; hippocampal systems support memory; hypothalamus regulates homeostasis; amygdala contributes to salience and threat learning.
concepts.advanced: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops and limbic circuits integrate cognition, affect, motor control and reinforcement. Subcortical structures are heterogeneous nuclei, not unitary emotion modules.
concepts.analogy: The city’s transport hub, security network, archive and utilities department operating beneath the visible skyline.
concepts.care: Subcortical dysfunction can mimic “purely psychological” problems through apathy, impulsivity, memory change, sleep disruption or altered emotional learning.
concepts.wrong: Degeneration, hypoxia, inflammation and focal injury may disrupt movement, memory, motivation or autonomic regulation.
concepts.pearl: Deep structures influence cortical processing continuously; “higher” does not mean independent.

quiz.question: Which structure is central to forming new episodic memories?
options: Hippocampus
Medulla
Primary motor cortex
Occipital pole
quiz.explanation: The hippocampal formation is crucial for encoding and consolidating new episodic memories.

concepts.title: Brainstem & Cerebellum
concepts.subtitle: Arousal, coordination and prediction
concepts.simple: The brainstem keeps vital systems running and helps you stay awake. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and helps the brain predict what happens next.
concepts.psych: Brainstem nuclei regulate arousal, sleep, autonomic function and cranial nerves. Cerebellar circuits contribute to timing, error correction, learning and aspects of cognition and affect.
concepts.advanced: Ascending neuromodulatory systems influence global cortical state. Cerebello-thalamo-cortical loops support predictive modelling beyond motor control, including language, executive and affective regulation.
concepts.analogy: The brainstem is the power-and-alertness system; the cerebellum is a precision coach constantly comparing intended and actual performance.
concepts.care: Arousal and autonomic state can profoundly shape attention, emotion regulation and test performance.
concepts.wrong: Damage may cause altered consciousness, cranial nerve signs, ataxia, dysmetria or cognitive-affective changes.
concepts.pearl: Before interpreting cognition, ask whether the person’s arousal and physiological state permit cognition to work normally.

quiz.question: Which structure is especially important for error correction and timing?
options: Cerebellum
Amygdala
Corpus callosum
Pituitary gland
quiz.explanation: The cerebellum compares predicted and actual outcomes to refine timing, coordination and learning.

concepts.title: Neurons
concepts.subtitle: The brain’s adaptive signalling specialists
concepts.simple: Neurons are living communication cells. Their branches receive many messages, the cell body weighs them together, and the axon sends a new signal when the combined input is strong enough. At the far end, the neuron usually turns that electrical signal into a chemical message for the next cell.
concepts.psych: A neuron performs input integration rather than simply relaying information. Excitatory, inhibitory and modulatory inputs arrive across dendrites and the soma; their timing, location and strength influence whether the axon initial segment reaches threshold. The resulting action potential carries output to synaptic terminals, where neurotransmitter release changes the probability that downstream cells will fire.
concepts.advanced: Neuronal function emerges from morphology, membrane conductances, receptor expression, axonal architecture and network position. Dendritic cable properties attenuate and filter synaptic currents, while active dendritic channels can amplify or compartmentalise inputs. The axon initial segment is enriched in voltage-gated sodium channels and acts as a dynamic trigger zone. Synaptic efficacy is altered through short- and long-term plasticity, homeostatic regulation and neuromodulatory state, meaning the same anatomical connection can have different functional consequences over time.
concepts.analogy: A neuron is closer to a busy emergency department than a copper wire. Thousands of messages arrive with different urgency, timing and credibility. The system integrates them, decides whether the threshold for action has been reached, and then sends a standardised alert to multiple downstream teams.
concepts.care: Psychological learning, memory and therapy-related change depend partly on altered synaptic weighting and network recruitment. However, behaviour should not be reduced to a single neuron or transmitter: cognition and emotion emerge from coordinated populations embedded in bodily and social contexts. Medications, sleep, stress hormones, inflammation and experience can all alter neuronal excitability and plasticity.
concepts.wrong: Neuronal signalling can fail through metabolic deprivation, excitotoxicity, axonal injury, abnormal synchrony, toxic exposure, neurodegeneration or disrupted development. The clinical expression depends less on one damaged cell than on which pathways and networks lose sufficient function or compensation. In epilepsy, for example, the central problem is pathological network synchronisation—not a lone “overactive neuron.”
concepts.pearl: The clinically meaningful unit is usually the circuit, but understanding the circuit requires knowing what each neuron can receive, compute, change and transmit.

quiz.question: Which neuronal part primarily carries action potentials away from the soma?
options: Axon
Dendrite
Nucleus
Synaptic cleft
quiz.explanation: The axon conducts action potentials from the cell body toward downstream targets.

concepts.title: Astrocytes
concepts.subtitle: Metabolic and synaptic partners
concepts.simple: Astrocytes are star-shaped cells that keep the neighbourhood around neurons safe and usable. They clear leftover chemical messages, balance charged particles, help provide fuel and connect active brain tissue with nearby blood vessels.
concepts.psych: Astrocytes actively regulate the extracellular environment in which neuronal signalling occurs. Their perisynaptic processes clear glutamate, buffer potassium, support the blood–brain barrier and coordinate metabolic and vascular responses to local neural activity.
concepts.advanced: Astrocytes occupy largely non-overlapping territories and extend fine processes around synapses and microvessels. EAAT transporters drive glutamate uptake and the glutamate–glutamine cycle; Kir channels and gap-junction coupling contribute to spatial potassium buffering. Vascular endfeet form a major component of the neurovascular unit. Astrocyte calcium and metabolic signalling are heterogeneous and context-dependent, so simplified claims that astrocytes merely 'feed' neurons or directly encode cognition should be avoided.
concepts.analogy: Astrocytes are the venue operations team around a live performance: they manage power, remove waste, control crowd conditions, restock supplies and signal when more resources are needed. The performers are visible, but the show fails without the systems around them.
concepts.care: Astrocytes matter whenever symptoms may reflect unstable excitability, impaired energy support, altered blood–brain barrier function or neuroinflammation. They also clarify why fMRI is an indirect measure: local blood-flow changes emerge from coordinated neuron–glia–vascular signalling rather than from neurons alone.
concepts.wrong: Astrocyte dysfunction can permit glutamate accumulation, impair potassium homeostasis, weaken metabolic support or alter neurovascular coupling. Reactive astrogliosis may contain damage and aid repair, but prolonged or dysregulated responses can also contribute to scarring, inflammation and network disturbance.
concepts.pearl: Neurons generate signals, but astrocytes help determine whether the surrounding tissue is stable enough for those signals to remain meaningful.

quiz.question: Which is a major astrocyte function?
options: Buffering extracellular potassium
Generating skeletal muscle force
Producing cerebrospinal fluid alone
Carrying visual images
quiz.explanation: Astrocytes help stabilise the extracellular ionic environment, including potassium buffering.

concepts.title: Microglia
concepts.subtitle: Immune surveillance and remodelling
concepts.simple: Microglia are the brain and spinal cord’s resident immune sentinels. Their branches constantly inspect nearby tissue, remove debris and help reshape connections when change is needed.
concepts.psych: Microglia coordinate surveillance, phagocytosis, inflammatory signalling and activity-dependent synaptic remodelling. Their function depends on developmental stage, region, prior exposure and the local molecular environment.
concepts.advanced: Microglia arise from yolk-sac progenitors and maintain themselves within the CNS. Their phenotypes are multidimensional and context-specific; binary labels such as resting/activated or M1/M2 obscure substantial transcriptional and functional diversity.
concepts.analogy: A combined neighbourhood watch, forensic team, waste-removal service and renovation crew. The job is not merely to attack—it is to inspect, decide, clear and restore proportionately.
concepts.care: Neuroimmune processes can influence cognition, fatigue and mood, but symptoms alone do not establish microglial dysfunction. Translational claims should distinguish human evidence from cellular and animal findings.
concepts.wrong: Insufficient clearance can prolong tissue stress, while excessive or persistent signalling may amplify inflammation, disrupt synapses or contribute to neurodegenerative cascades.
concepts.pearl: Microglia are neither heroes nor villains. The clinical question is what state they are in, why, for how long, and with what effect on the surrounding network.

quiz.question: Microglia are best described as the brain’s…
options: Resident immune cells
Primary myelinating cells in the CNS
Main excitatory neurons
Hormone-producing gland
quiz.explanation: Microglia are the resident innate immune cells of the central nervous system.

concepts.title: Oligodendrocytes
concepts.subtitle: Myelin builders of the CNS
concepts.simple: Oligodendrocytes are specialised glial cells that wrap central nervous system axons in myelin. The wrap leaves tiny gaps so electrical signals can leap efficiently from one gap to the next.
concepts.psych: One oligodendrocyte can form myelin internodes on several CNS axons. Myelin increases membrane resistance and reduces capacitance, enabling saltatory conduction while oligodendrocytes also provide metabolic support to the axons they ensheath.
concepts.advanced: Compact myelin is a multilamellar extension of oligodendrocyte membrane. Nodal, paranodal and juxtaparanodal domains organise ion channels and axoglial junctions so depolarising current spreads rapidly beneath internodes and action potentials regenerate at nodes of Ranvier. Activity-dependent changes in oligodendrogenesis and sheath properties may contribute to experience-dependent circuit timing.
concepts.analogy: A high-speed rail line: insulated track carries traffic quickly between precisely spaced stations, where the signal is actively renewed.
concepts.care: White matter supports the timing and integration of distributed cognitive systems. Disruption may appear as slowed processing, fatigue, variable attention or reduced coordination across functions rather than a single neat localisation.
concepts.wrong: Demyelination, failed remyelination or loss of oligodendrocyte metabolic support can slow conduction, cause conduction block and increase axonal vulnerability. Clinical effects depend on pathway, lesion burden and network compensation.
concepts.pearl: Myelin is not passive wrapping. It is living, maintained tissue that shapes when signals arrive—and cognition depends heavily on timing.

quiz.question: What is the main function of CNS myelin?
options: Increase speed and reliability of axonal conduction
Create neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft
Store episodic memories
Control pituitary hormones
quiz.explanation: Myelin enables rapid saltatory conduction and supports axonal function.

concepts.title: Resting Membrane Potential
concepts.subtitle: The voltage before a neuron fires
concepts.simple: A resting neuron is not switched off. It actively keeps more positive charge outside than inside, creating a small electrical difference across its membrane.
concepts.psych: Resting membrane potential is the baseline voltage from which excitatory and inhibitory inputs shift a neuron toward or away from threshold. It reflects ion gradients, selective permeability and ongoing pump activity.
concepts.advanced: At rest, neuronal membranes are most permeable to potassium through leak channels. Potassium efflux leaves the intracellular space relatively negative, while impermeant anions and smaller sodium permeability shape the final voltage. Na+/K+-ATPase maintains the gradients that make this equilibrium possible rather than directly generating each moment of voltage.
concepts.analogy: A charged battery held ready: energy has already been invested to separate charge, so a signal can be generated quickly when the circuit changes.
concepts.care: Resting potential determines excitability. Electrolyte disturbance, channel dysfunction, hypoxia and medications that alter conductance can change arousal, cognition, seizure threshold and motor function.
concepts.wrong: If ion gradients collapse or the membrane becomes persistently depolarised, neurons may fail to fire normally, become hyperexcitable or enter depolarisation block.
concepts.pearl: “Resting” describes the absence of an action potential—not metabolic inactivity.

quiz.question: Which ion has the greatest influence on a typical neuron’s resting membrane potential?
options: Potassium
Calcium
Chloride only
Magnesium
quiz.explanation: Resting conductance is usually dominated by potassium leak channels.

concepts.title: Action Potentials
concepts.subtitle: The neuron’s regenerative electrical signal
concepts.simple: When enough input reaches threshold, a neuron produces a brief electrical pulse that travels along its axon without fading.
concepts.psych: Action potentials convert graded synaptic input into a reliable all-or-none axonal output. Information is represented less by pulse size than by firing timing, rate and pattern.
concepts.advanced: Threshold recruits voltage-gated sodium channels, generating rapid depolarisation through positive feedback. Sodium-channel inactivation and delayed potassium-channel opening repolarise the membrane. Absolute and relative refractory periods constrain maximum firing rate and direction of propagation.
concepts.analogy: A row of mousetraps: once one snaps, it triggers the next. Each section regenerates the same event rather than passing a weakening spark.
concepts.care: Many anaesthetics, anti-seizure agents and toxins alter voltage-gated channels. Conduction timing also affects synchrony across distributed cognitive networks.
concepts.wrong: Channelopathies, demyelination, ischemia and electrolyte disturbance may cause ectopic firing, slowed conduction or conduction failure.
concepts.pearl: Action potentials are all-or-none locally, but neural coding is richly graded across time and populations.

quiz.question: What directly produces the rapid upstroke of an action potential?
options: Voltage-gated sodium entry
Passive chloride storage
Myelin synthesis
Neurotransmitter reuptake
quiz.explanation: Rapid sodium influx drives the depolarising upstroke.

concepts.title: Synapses
concepts.subtitle: Where one cell changes another
concepts.simple: A synapse is a tiny communication point where one cell influences the next using chemicals or direct electrical flow.
concepts.psych: Synapses transform presynaptic activity into postsynaptic change. Their strength, timing and location determine whether inputs are excitatory, inhibitory or modulatory in a particular circuit.
concepts.advanced: At chemical synapses, presynaptic calcium entry triggers SNARE-dependent vesicle fusion. Transmitter diffuses across the cleft and activates ionotropic or metabotropic receptors. Signal duration is limited by diffusion, enzymatic breakdown and transporter-mediated uptake. Electrical synapses use gap junctions for direct current flow.
concepts.analogy: A highly regulated handover desk: the sender packages a message, releases it into a narrow gap, and the receiver interprets it using specialised readers.
concepts.care: Most psychotropic medications alter synaptic signalling through receptors, transporters, enzymes or release mechanisms. Synaptic plasticity is also central to learning and therapy-related change.
concepts.wrong: Excess release, receptor dysfunction, impaired clearance or autoimmune attack on synaptic proteins can disturb cognition, mood, movement and consciousness.
concepts.pearl: A neurotransmitter is not inherently “excitatory” or “inhibitory”; its effect depends on receptor, cell and circuit context.

quiz.question: What directly triggers synaptic vesicle fusion?
options: Presynaptic calcium entry
Potassium storage in myelin
Nuclear transcription alone
Astrocyte cell division
quiz.explanation: Calcium entering through voltage-gated channels activates fusion machinery.

concepts.title: Neurotransmitters
concepts.subtitle: Chemical signals with context-dependent effects
concepts.simple: Neurotransmitters are chemicals neurons release to influence other cells. Their meaning depends on which receptor receives them and where that receptor sits in the network.
concepts.psych: Transmitters organise communication across fast excitation, inhibition and slower neuromodulation. Clinical interpretation requires receptor- and circuit-level reasoning rather than assigning one emotion or diagnosis to one chemical.
concepts.advanced: Classical transmitters are synthesised, stored, released in a calcium-dependent manner and cleared through transporters, enzymes or diffusion. Glutamate and GABA dominate fast cortical excitation and inhibition, while dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and acetylcholine often modulate gain, salience, plasticity and state across distributed projections.
concepts.analogy: The chemical is a word, the receptor is the language, and the circuit is the conversation. The same word can mean different things in different contexts.
concepts.care: Medication effects depend on dose, receptor subtype, baseline state, region, timescale and adaptation. “Low serotonin” or “too much dopamine” explanations are usually clinically inadequate.
concepts.wrong: Imbalanced release, receptor sensitivity, clearance or network regulation can contribute to seizures, movement disorders, psychosis, mood symptoms and cognitive change—but rarely as a single-cause story.
concepts.pearl: Transmitters do not carry diagnoses. Circuits, timing, receptors and context determine functional meaning.

quiz.question: Why can the same neurotransmitter have different effects?
options: Different receptor subtypes and circuits interpret it differently
Its molecules change colour in each brain region
Transmitters have no receptors
Only glia determine all effects
quiz.explanation: Receptor coupling and circuit context determine functional effect.

concepts.title: Neuroplasticity
concepts.subtitle: How experience changes neural systems
concepts.simple: The brain changes with experience. Connections can strengthen, weaken, reorganise or become easier to activate through learning and repetition.
concepts.psych: Plasticity includes synaptic, intrinsic, structural and network-level adaptation. It supports learning and recovery, but also the persistence of fear, pain, avoidance and maladaptive habits.
concepts.advanced: Long-term potentiation and depression alter synaptic efficacy through receptor trafficking, kinase signalling, gene expression and structural remodelling. Homeostatic plasticity stabilises activity, while metaplasticity changes the rules by which future plasticity occurs. Systems consolidation redistributes memory dependence over time.
concepts.analogy: A landscape of paths: repeated travel makes some routes faster and more automatic, while unused routes become harder to find. New routes are possible, but terrain and repetition matter.
concepts.care: Psychotherapy, rehabilitation, exposure, skills practice and environmental change all rely on experience-dependent updating. Plasticity is constrained—not magical—and requires sufficiently repeated, salient and tolerable learning.
concepts.wrong: The same mechanisms can reinforce avoidance, compulsions, sensitisation, addiction and chronic pain. Change can also be destabilising if arousal overwhelms learning capacity.
concepts.pearl: “The brain can change” is true; “the brain can change instantly, without constraints or practice” is not.

quiz.question: What is long-term potentiation?
options: A durable increase in synaptic efficacy after particular activity patterns
Permanent firing of every neuron
Loss of all inhibitory transmission
Immediate growth of an entire brain region
quiz.explanation: LTP is a sustained strengthening of synaptic transmission.

concepts.title: Functional Networks
concepts.subtitle: The brain works through coordinated systems
concepts.simple: Brain regions rarely act alone. Functional networks are groups of areas whose activity changes together while the brain rests or performs a task.
concepts.psych: Network neuroscience shifts interpretation from isolated “centres” toward distributed, dynamically coupled systems. A region can participate in more than one network depending on context and task demand.
concepts.advanced: Functional connectivity describes statistical dependence between signals; it does not by itself prove direct anatomical connection or causal influence. Network organisation is multiscale, partly overlapping and state dependent.
concepts.analogy: Think of an orchestra: individual instruments matter, but the meaningful unit is the coordinated pattern they form together.
concepts.care: Symptoms such as distractibility, rumination or cognitive inflexibility often reflect altered coordination among systems rather than failure of one structure.
concepts.wrong: Network disruption can follow focal lesions, diffuse injury, neurodevelopmental variation, sleep loss, stress or psychiatric illness. Similar symptoms can arise from different network mechanisms.
concepts.pearl: A bright spot on a scan is not a psychological faculty. Ask what network, task, comparison and behavioural process the signal belongs to.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects this concept?
options: It depends on distributed, context-sensitive network coordination
It is produced by one isolated brain centre
It can be diagnosed from a single scan
It is unaffected by task or state
quiz.explanation: Modern network neuroscience emphasises distributed and state-dependent coordination.

concepts.title: Default Mode Network
concepts.subtitle: Internal simulation, memory and self-related thought
concepts.simple: The Default Mode Network becomes prominent when attention turns inward—remembering, imagining, reflecting on yourself or making sense of other people.
concepts.psych: The DMN supports autobiographical memory, future simulation, semantic integration and aspects of social cognition. It is not simply an “inactive” or daydreaming network.
concepts.advanced: Core nodes commonly include medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate/precuneus and angular or lateral temporal regions. The network fractionates into subsystems and changes coupling across tasks.
concepts.analogy: It is the brain’s internal story room: a place where past experience is recombined to model the self, other people and possible futures.
concepts.care: DMN dynamics are relevant to rumination, trauma-related self-processing, depression, dissociation, social cognition and psychotherapy narratives.
concepts.wrong: Excessive persistence, weak task-related suppression or abnormal coupling may accompany rumination and attentional difficulty, but findings are heterogeneous and not diagnostic.
concepts.pearl: The DMN is not “the ego network.” It is a distributed system with several functions, and its activity must be interpreted in context.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects this concept?
options: It depends on distributed, context-sensitive network coordination
It is produced by one isolated brain centre
It can be diagnosed from a single scan
It is unaffected by task or state
quiz.explanation: Modern network neuroscience emphasises distributed and state-dependent coordination.

concepts.title: Salience Network
concepts.subtitle: Detecting what matters and coordinating a switch
concepts.simple: The Salience Network helps notice what is important—inside the body or in the environment—and recruits the systems needed to respond.
concepts.psych: Anchored around anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate, the network integrates interoceptive, emotional and cognitive signals and may help shift between internally and externally oriented processing.
concepts.advanced: Salience is not identical to danger. It reflects behavioural relevance. The network interacts with autonomic, limbic, sensory and control systems, and its boundaries vary across parcellations.
concepts.analogy: It is the brain’s triage nurse: it does not do every job, but it decides what needs attention now and who should be called in.
concepts.care: Salience processing is central to anxiety, panic, trauma, addiction, pain, psychosis and interoceptive awareness.
concepts.wrong: Hyper-responsive salience detection may amplify threat or bodily sensations; under-responsive signalling may reduce engagement. Either pattern can be context-dependent rather than globally abnormal.
concepts.pearl: When everything feels urgent, the problem may be prioritisation—not simply “too much emotion.”

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects this concept?
options: It depends on distributed, context-sensitive network coordination
It is produced by one isolated brain centre
It can be diagnosed from a single scan
It is unaffected by task or state
quiz.explanation: Modern network neuroscience emphasises distributed and state-dependent coordination.

concepts.title: Frontoparietal Control Network
concepts.subtitle: Flexible goals, rules and adaptive control
concepts.simple: The Frontoparietal Control Network helps hold goals in mind, adjust plans and coordinate other brain systems when a task is difficult or new.
concepts.psych: Distributed lateral prefrontal and parietal regions support flexible cognitive control, working-memory operations and context-sensitive coordination across networks.
concepts.advanced: The network is heterogeneous and sometimes divided into multiple control systems. It adapts rapidly to task demands and often couples with either default-mode or attention systems depending on the goal.
concepts.analogy: It is an executive project team that assembles the right specialists, updates the plan and reallocates effort when conditions change.
concepts.care: Its functions are relevant to executive assessment, ADHD, depression, acquired brain injury, cognitive fatigue and treatment planning.
concepts.wrong: Reduced efficiency can appear as inconsistent performance, poor set shifting, weak monitoring or overload under complexity. High effort may preserve accuracy while increasing fatigue.
concepts.pearl: Executive difficulty is often a coordination problem under demand, not proof that a person lacks knowledge, motivation or intelligence.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects this concept?
options: It depends on distributed, context-sensitive network coordination
It is produced by one isolated brain centre
It can be diagnosed from a single scan
It is unaffected by task or state
quiz.explanation: Modern network neuroscience emphasises distributed and state-dependent coordination.

concepts.title: Attention Networks
concepts.subtitle: Selecting, sustaining and reorienting attention
concepts.simple: Attention is not one spotlight. Several systems help maintain readiness, select a target and redirect focus when something important appears.
concepts.psych: Dorsal frontoparietal systems support goal-directed selection, while ventral attention regions—especially right-lateralised—help interrupt and reorient toward behaviourally relevant events.
concepts.advanced: Alerting, orienting and executive control are partially separable. Attention fluctuates with arousal, motivation, task structure and network coupling; no single network explains all attentional symptoms.
concepts.analogy: It is a camera crew: one system aims the lens, another watches for unexpected events, and a third keeps the whole production on task.
concepts.care: Network-level attention models improve formulation of ADHD, neglect, anxiety-related scanning, trauma vigilance and post-injury attentional fatigue.
concepts.wrong: Damage or dysregulation can produce neglect, distractibility, hypervigilance, slowed disengagement or poor sustained attention. Behaviour alone does not identify the exact mechanism.
concepts.pearl: “Inattention” is an outcome. Clinically, ask whether the bottleneck is alertness, selection, disengagement, control, reward or overload.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects this concept?
options: It depends on distributed, context-sensitive network coordination
It is produced by one isolated brain centre
It can be diagnosed from a single scan
It is unaffected by task or state
quiz.explanation: Modern network neuroscience emphasises distributed and state-dependent coordination.

concepts.title: Embryonic Neural Development
concepts.subtitle: From a sheet of cells to a patterned nervous system
concepts.simple: Early in development, signals tell a small sheet of cells to become nervous tissue. Those cells then organise into regions that will later form the brain and spinal cord.
concepts.psych: Neural development begins through induction and patterning. Molecular gradients establish body axes, regional identity and the progenitor zones from which neurons and glia emerge.
concepts.advanced: Ectodermal cells adopt neural fate as BMP signalling is inhibited. Rostrocaudal and dorsoventral morphogen gradients—including WNT, FGF, retinoic acid and sonic hedgehog—specify progenitor identities before mature structures exist.
concepts.analogy: It is like zoning a new city before roads or buildings are constructed: location determines which specialised neighbourhood each plot can become.
concepts.care: Developmental timing helps explain why early insults can produce broad neurodevelopmental effects, while later insults may affect narrower circuits or skills.
concepts.wrong: Genetic variants, teratogens, placental compromise and severe nutritional deficiency can disrupt induction, patterning, proliferation or differentiation.
concepts.pearl: Development is not the simple unfolding of a blueprint; genes, cellular signals, activity and environment continually constrain one another.

quiz.question: Neural induction most directly refers to:
options: Ectoderm adopting a neural fate
Axons forming myelin
Synapses being pruned
The cortex producing EEG
quiz.explanation: Neural induction is the early commitment of ectodermal cells toward nervous-system tissue.

concepts.title: Neural Tube Formation
concepts.subtitle: Folding the future brain and spinal cord
concepts.simple: The early nervous system begins as a flat sheet. Its edges rise, meet and close to create a hollow tube that becomes the brain and spinal cord.
concepts.psych: Neurulation transforms the neural plate into the neural tube. Closure proceeds along the body axis, while neural crest cells separate and contribute to peripheral structures.
concepts.advanced: Primary neurulation depends on coordinated cell-shape change, hinge-point formation and neural-fold elevation. Neuropores close at defined times; folate-dependent one-carbon metabolism is clinically important because failed closure can cause neural-tube defects.
concepts.analogy: Imagine rolling a flexible map into a sealed tunnel, while selected travellers peel away from its edges to build systems outside the tunnel.
concepts.care: This process links developmental biology to prevention: periconceptional folic acid substantially reduces the risk of many neural-tube defects.
concepts.wrong: Incomplete closure may produce anencephaly, encephalocele or spina bifida, with severity depending on location and extent.
concepts.pearl: By the time many people know they are pregnant, neural-tube closure has largely occurred—prevention must begin before conception.

quiz.question: The neural tube later forms the:
options: Brain and spinal cord
Skull and vertebrae only
Peripheral muscles
Placenta
quiz.explanation: The central nervous system develops from the neural tube.

concepts.title: Neuronal Migration
concepts.subtitle: Getting new neurons to the correct layer
concepts.simple: Many young neurons are born deep in the developing brain, then travel to the place where they will work. Their destination matters as much as their identity.
concepts.psych: Cortical neurons migrate from proliferative zones along radial glial scaffolds or through tangential routes. Migration establishes cortical layers and positions inhibitory interneurons within emerging circuits.
concepts.advanced: Excitatory projection neurons predominantly migrate radially in an inside-out sequence, while many GABAergic interneurons migrate tangentially from ventral progenitor zones. Guidance cues, adhesion molecules and cytoskeletal dynamics coordinate locomotion and final placement.
concepts.analogy: It is like assigning clinicians to the right floor of a hospital: the correct professional in the wrong ward cannot contribute to the intended team.
concepts.care: Migration disorders illustrate why normal cell number does not guarantee normal function; misplaced neurons can alter excitability, connectivity and cognition.
concepts.wrong: Disrupted migration can contribute to lissencephaly, heterotopia, focal cortical dysplasia, epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment.
concepts.pearl: Cortical layering is a developmental history written into anatomy: deeper neurons generally arrive before more superficial neurons.

quiz.question: Radial glia are important because they:
options: Act as progenitors and migration scaffolds
Form adult skull bone
Carry hormones in blood
Generate cerebrospinal fluid only
quiz.explanation: Radial glia both produce cells and guide migration.

concepts.title: Synaptogenesis
concepts.subtitle: Building and refining neural connections
concepts.simple: Developing neurons grow branches and form huge numbers of connections. Activity and experience then help keep useful connections and weaken others.
concepts.psych: Synaptogenesis is the formation and maturation of synaptic contacts. It occurs in overlapping waves, followed by activity-dependent stabilisation, competition and pruning.
concepts.advanced: Axon guidance brings presynaptic and postsynaptic partners into proximity. Adhesion molecules and trans-synaptic organisers align release machinery with receptor-rich postsynaptic densities. Subsequent activity influences receptor composition, spine morphology and circuit retention.
concepts.analogy: It resembles creating an enormous draft contact list, then repeatedly testing which connections are reliable, relevant and worth maintaining.
concepts.care: Experience-expectant development depends on common inputs during sensitive periods, while experience-dependent plasticity continues to encode individual learning.
concepts.wrong: Disrupted synapse formation, excitation–inhibition balance or pruning is implicated across several neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, but findings are heterogeneous and not diagnosis-specific.
concepts.pearl: Pruning is not simply loss; it is selective refinement that can increase efficiency and signal-to-noise.

quiz.question: Synaptogenesis refers to:
options: Formation and maturation of synaptic contacts
Closure of the neural tube
Production of cerebrospinal fluid
Only adult memory retrieval
quiz.explanation: Synaptogenesis builds functional junctions between cells.

concepts.title: Developmental Myelination
concepts.subtitle: Insulating axons as networks mature
concepts.simple: Myelin wraps around many axons like insulation. It helps signals travel faster and more reliably, and it continues developing for many years.
concepts.psych: Myelination is a prolonged, regionally patterned process. Oligodendrocytes in the CNS add sheaths to selected axons, supporting conduction speed, timing precision and metabolic resilience.
concepts.advanced: Myelin formation begins prenatally in some pathways but continues through childhood, adolescence and adulthood. Internode length, sheath thickness and nodal organisation are adapted to axon calibre and circuit demands. Experience can influence oligodendrocyte generation and sheath remodelling.
concepts.analogy: It is like upgrading roads from rough tracks to timed express lanes: information arrives faster, with less variability and better coordination across distant regions.
concepts.care: Protracted myelination helps explain why processing speed, executive control and long-range coordination continue developing beyond early childhood.
concepts.wrong: Hypoxic injury, inflammation, genetic leukodystrophies and nutritional deficiencies can disrupt white-matter development; interpretation requires developmental and medical context.
concepts.pearl: Myelination does not simply make the brain “faster”—it tunes the timing relationships that allow distributed networks to work together.

quiz.question: The primary myelinating cell of the CNS is the:
options: Oligodendrocyte
Astrocyte
Microglial cell
Ependymal cell
quiz.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin.

concepts.title: Hippocampus
concepts.subtitle: Binding experiences into relational and episodic memory
concepts.simple: The hippocampus helps connect the who, what, where and when of an experience so it can later be remembered as an event.
concepts.psych: The hippocampal formation supports rapid relational learning, episodic memory and spatial-contextual representation. It works with distributed cortical systems rather than storing complete memories in isolation.
concepts.advanced: Dentate gyrus pattern separation, CA3 recurrent circuitry and CA1 comparison processes support discrimination, completion and temporal-context coding. Consolidation involves coordinated hippocampal–neocortical replay across wake and sleep.
concepts.analogy: It is less like a storage box and more like an expert librarian that rapidly indexes how parts of an experience belong together.
concepts.care: Hippocampal dysfunction can present as impaired new learning, context confusion and difficulty binding details across time and place.
concepts.wrong: Bilateral medial temporal damage can cause profound anterograde amnesia. Chronic stress, seizures, hypoxia and neurodegenerative disease may impair hippocampal function, although reduced volume is not diagnostically specific.
concepts.pearl: The hippocampus is crucial for forming relational memories, but durable knowledge is distributed across wider cortical networks.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Hippocampus?
options: The hippocampus helps connect the who, what, where and when of an experience so it can later be remembered as an event.
It performs one isolated function without network input
It is only active during sleep
It is a peripheral nervous system structure
quiz.explanation: The hippocampal formation supports rapid relational learning, episodic memory and spatial-contextual representation. It works with distributed cortical systems rather than storing complete memories in isolation.

concepts.title: Amygdala
concepts.subtitle: Assigning emotional and motivational significance
concepts.simple: The amygdala helps the brain notice what matters, especially cues linked with danger, reward or strong emotion.
concepts.psych: The amygdala is a collection of nuclei that supports salience learning, threat conditioning, emotional memory modulation and rapid coordination of behavioural and autonomic responses.
concepts.advanced: Basolateral nuclei integrate sensory and contextual inputs and update cue value; central nuclei coordinate hypothalamic and brainstem effectors. Amygdala–prefrontal–hippocampal loops enable context-sensitive regulation rather than a simple fear centre.
concepts.analogy: It is a significance detector and learning amplifier, not a single-purpose panic button.
concepts.care: Amygdala processes contribute to fear learning, avoidance, reward learning, trauma responses and emotionally enhanced memory.
concepts.wrong: Hyperreactivity, impaired extinction or weak contextual regulation may contribute to anxiety and trauma symptoms, but imaging findings are probabilistic and not individually diagnostic.
concepts.pearl: The amygdala signals relevance; whether that signal becomes adaptive action depends on context and regulation across the wider network.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Amygdala?
options: The amygdala helps the brain notice what matters, especially cues linked with danger, reward or strong emotion.
It performs one isolated function without network input
It is only active during sleep
It is a peripheral nervous system structure
quiz.explanation: The amygdala is a collection of nuclei that supports salience learning, threat conditioning, emotional memory modulation and rapid coordination of behavioural and autonomic responses.

concepts.title: Corpus Callosum
concepts.subtitle: Coordinating information between cerebral hemispheres
concepts.simple: The corpus callosum is the brain’s largest bridge, carrying information between the left and right hemispheres.
concepts.psych: Callosal fibres enable interhemispheric integration, transfer and inhibition. Different sectors connect homologous and non-homologous cortical regions with distinct developmental trajectories.
concepts.advanced: Approximately 200 million myelinated axons form topographically organised callosal pathways. Conduction timing, axon calibre and myelination influence bilateral synchrony and competition.
concepts.analogy: It is a high-capacity fibre-optic bridge that lets two specialised teams share information without becoming identical.
concepts.care: Callosal integrity matters for bilateral sensory integration, motor coordination, language, social cognition and distributed executive control.
concepts.wrong: Agenesis, demyelination, traumatic injury or surgical section can produce disconnection syndromes, though outcomes vary with timing and compensatory pathways.
concepts.pearl: Interhemispheric communication is not simply “left brain versus right brain”; most complex functions depend on coordinated bilateral networks.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Corpus Callosum?
options: The corpus callosum is the brain’s largest bridge, carrying information between the left and right hemispheres.
It performs one isolated function without network input
It is only active during sleep
It is a peripheral nervous system structure
quiz.explanation: Callosal fibres enable interhemispheric integration, transfer and inhibition. Different sectors connect homologous and non-homologous cortical regions with distinct developmental trajectories.

concepts.title: Ventricular System
concepts.subtitle: Producing and circulating cerebrospinal fluid
concepts.simple: The ventricles are connected fluid-filled spaces that cushion the brain and help circulate nutrients and waste products.
concepts.psych: The ventricular system contains cerebrospinal fluid produced mainly by the choroid plexus. CSF circulates through ventricles and subarachnoid spaces before reabsorption into venous and lymphatic pathways.
concepts.advanced: Lateral ventricles drain via the foramina of Monro to the third ventricle, then through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle. Pressure depends on production, flow, compliance and outflow resistance.
concepts.analogy: It is a protected internal plumbing and suspension system running through the brain.
concepts.care: Ventricular size and CSF flow are relevant in hydrocephalus, intracranial pressure, infection, haemorrhage and some neurodegenerative conditions.
concepts.wrong: Obstruction or impaired reabsorption can cause hydrocephalus. Ventricular enlargement may reflect pressure, tissue loss or developmental variation and must be interpreted in context.
concepts.pearl: Large ventricles are a structural observation, not a diagnosis; the mechanism and clinical context determine significance.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Ventricular System?
options: The ventricles are connected fluid-filled spaces that cushion the brain and help circulate nutrients and waste products.
It performs one isolated function without network input
It is only active during sleep
It is a peripheral nervous system structure
quiz.explanation: The ventricular system contains cerebrospinal fluid produced mainly by the choroid plexus. CSF circulates through ventricles and subarachnoid spaces before reabsorption into venous and lymphatic pathways.

concepts.title: Blood–Brain Barrier
concepts.subtitle: Regulating exchange between blood and neural tissue
concepts.simple: The blood–brain barrier is a selective filter that protects the brain while still allowing essential nutrients to enter.
concepts.psych: Brain endothelial tight junctions, pericytes, basement membrane and astrocytic end-feet form a neurovascular unit that tightly regulates molecular and cellular traffic.
concepts.advanced: Transport occurs through selective carriers, receptor-mediated transcytosis and controlled paracellular restriction. Barrier properties vary by region and change with inflammation, development and disease.
concepts.analogy: It is a highly selective border crossing staffed by specialised cells, not an impenetrable wall.
concepts.care: Barrier function affects medication delivery, neuroinflammation, oedema, infection and the interpretation of peripheral biomarkers.
concepts.wrong: Disruption can permit plasma proteins, immune mediators and fluid to enter neural tissue, contributing to oedema and altered excitability. However, “leaky brain” claims often exceed available evidence.
concepts.pearl: The barrier protects neural stability, but it is dynamic and communicates continuously with the immune and vascular systems.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Blood–Brain Barrier?
options: The blood–brain barrier is a selective filter that protects the brain while still allowing essential nutrients to enter.
It performs one isolated function without network input
It is only active during sleep
It is a peripheral nervous system structure
quiz.explanation: Brain endothelial tight junctions, pericytes, basement membrane and astrocytic end-feet form a neurovascular unit that tightly regulates molecular and cellular traffic.

concepts.title: Meninges
concepts.subtitle: Protective layers around brain and spinal cord
concepts.simple: The brain and spinal cord are wrapped in three protective layers. These layers cushion delicate tissue, contain fluid spaces and help organise blood vessels around the nervous system.
concepts.psych: The dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater form a layered protective system. Their spaces matter clinically because blood, infection or altered cerebrospinal-fluid pressure can affect neural function without beginning inside brain tissue itself.
concepts.advanced: The pachymeninges consist primarily of dura, while the leptomeninges comprise arachnoid and pia. The subarachnoid space contains cerebrospinal fluid, arteries and bridging trabeculae. Dural venous sinuses drain cerebral veins and CSF via arachnoid granulations. Potential epidural and subdural spaces become clinically apparent when blood or pathology separates tissue planes.
concepts.analogy: A high-value instrument packed in three specialised protective sleeves: a tough outer case, a webbed shock-absorbing layer and a delicate lining fitted directly to every contour.
concepts.care: Headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, altered consciousness and focal deficits may reflect meningeal inflammation, haemorrhage or pressure disturbance rather than a primary psychiatric process.
concepts.wrong: Meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, subdural haematoma and intracranial hypotension can rapidly alter cognition, behaviour and arousal.
concepts.pearl: When mental-state change is accompanied by severe headache, fever, meningism or abrupt neurological symptoms, treat it as neurological until proven otherwise.

quiz.question: Which component is best described as: Tough outer layer?
options: Dura mater
Arachnoid mater
Subarachnoid space
Pia mater
quiz.explanation: Dense connective tissue stabilises the cranial contents and forms venous sinuses.

concepts.title: Cranial Nerves
concepts.subtitle: Twelve paired pathways for sensation, movement and regulation
concepts.simple: Twelve pairs of nerves connect the brain directly with the eyes, face, ears, tongue, throat and internal organs. They let you see, smell, hear, move your face and regulate vital body functions.
concepts.psych: Cranial nerves provide a compact neurological screen of brainstem, sensory and motor integrity. Abnormal eye movements, facial asymmetry, dysarthria, swallowing difficulty or altered hearing can localise dysfunction and should not be reduced to anxiety without examination.
concepts.advanced: Cranial nerves I and II arise from forebrain structures; III–XII emerge primarily from brainstem nuclei. Their modalities include special sensory, somatic motor, branchial motor, visceral sensory and parasympathetic efferents. Because nuclei and fascicles are densely organised, combined deficits can identify midbrain, pontine or medullary lesions.
concepts.analogy: A twelve-cable control panel: some cables carry camera and microphone input, some drive facial and eye motors, and others quietly regulate organs in the background.
concepts.care: Cranial-nerve findings can distinguish panic-like dizziness, functional symptoms and medication effects from stroke, mass lesions, demyelination or peripheral neuropathy.
concepts.wrong: Brainstem stroke, raised intracranial pressure, Bell palsy, vestibular neuritis and compressive lesions can produce characteristic cranial-nerve patterns.
concepts.pearl: A single symptom is vague; a pattern across multiple cranial nerves is anatomical information.

quiz.question: Which component is best described as: Smell, vision and hearing/balance?
options: Sensory nerves I, II, VIII
Eye-movement nerves III, IV, VI
Trigeminal nerve V
Facial nerve VII
quiz.explanation: Carry special sensory information into the brain.

concepts.title: Visual System
concepts.subtitle: From retinal light detection to perception and action
concepts.simple: Your eyes turn light into nerve signals. Those signals cross and split so both halves of the brain can build a stable picture of the world and guide attention and movement.
concepts.psych: Vision is a distributed process involving retina, optic pathways, thalamus, primary visual cortex and dorsal and ventral association streams. Perception is an active inference shaped by attention, expectation and context—not a camera-like copy.
concepts.advanced: Retinal ganglion axons form the optic nerves; nasal fibres decussate at the optic chiasm, preserving contralateral visual hemifields. Most fibres synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus before optic radiations reach V1. Ventral occipitotemporal pathways support object identity, while dorsal occipitoparietal pathways support spatial guidance and visually directed action.
concepts.analogy: A live production studio: the retina captures raw footage, the thalamus routes feeds, early cortex extracts edges and contrast, and specialist teams identify what is present and where it is.
concepts.care: Visual complaints may reflect ocular disease, migraine, neglect, field loss, perceptual disturbance, medication effects or functional symptoms. Careful phenomenology prevents premature psychiatric attribution.
concepts.wrong: Optic neuritis, chiasmal compression, occipital stroke, visual neglect and agnosia produce distinct deficits depending on lesion location.
concepts.pearl: Ask what is lost: acuity, field, recognition, spatial attention or confidence in perception. Each points to a different system.

quiz.question: Which component is best described as: Transduces light into neural signals?
options: Retina
Optic chiasm
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Primary visual cortex
quiz.explanation: Photoreceptors and retinal circuits encode contrast, colour and timing.

concepts.title: Auditory System
concepts.subtitle: Turning vibration into sound, speech and spatial meaning
concepts.simple: Sound waves vibrate the inner ear, where tiny sensory cells turn movement into nerve signals. Brainstem and cortical pathways compare timing and loudness so you can recognise sounds and locate where they came from.
concepts.psych: Auditory perception depends on cochlear transduction, bilateral brainstem pathways, thalamic relay and temporal-cortical analysis. Speech, music and environmental meaning emerge from distributed networks shaped by attention and prediction.
concepts.advanced: Hair cells in the organ of Corti transduce basilar-membrane motion into auditory-nerve firing. Cochlear nuclei project bilaterally through superior olivary complexes, lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus and primary auditory cortex. Tonotopy is maintained across the pathway; interaural timing and level differences support spatial localisation.
concepts.analogy: A multistage audio studio: the cochlea separates frequencies, brainstem mixers compare left and right channels, and cortex identifies voices, language, music and significance.
concepts.care: Hearing loss can masquerade as inattention, social withdrawal, cognitive decline or noncompliance. Tinnitus and auditory hallucinations require different phenomenological and medical assessment.
concepts.wrong: Conductive or sensorineural hearing loss, auditory neuropathy, temporal-lobe lesions and central processing disorders affect different stages of the pathway.
concepts.pearl: Before interpreting reduced responsiveness psychologically, establish whether the person reliably received the signal.

quiz.question: Which component is best described as: Frequency analysis and transduction?
options: Cochlea
Auditory nerve
Superior olivary complex
Inferior colliculus
quiz.explanation: Basilar-membrane mechanics separate frequencies; hair cells encode vibration.

concepts.title: Somatosensory System
concepts.subtitle: Touch, body position, temperature and pain
concepts.simple: Your skin, muscles and joints constantly report touch, pressure, temperature, pain and body position. The spinal cord, thalamus and cortex combine these signals into a map of your body.
concepts.psych: Somatosensation includes discriminative touch, proprioception, nociception and temperature. Perception depends on ascending pathways plus attention, expectation, emotion and prior learning, which is why pain is real without being a simple readout of tissue damage.
concepts.advanced: Dorsal-column–medial-lemniscal pathways carry fine touch, vibration and conscious proprioception, decussating in the medulla. Anterolateral pathways carry nociceptive and thermal information, crossing near spinal entry. Thalamocortical projections reach primary and secondary somatosensory cortex, insula and cingulate regions, integrating sensory-discriminative and affective dimensions.
concepts.analogy: A body-wide sensor network: different cables carry texture, position, heat and threat signals, while the brain’s control room decides what deserves awareness and action.
concepts.care: Pain, numbness, dissociation and functional sensory symptoms require both neurological localisation and contextual formulation. “Top-down influence” does not mean imagined or voluntary.
concepts.wrong: Peripheral neuropathy, spinal-cord lesions, thalamic stroke, cortical lesions and central sensitisation produce different patterns of sensory change.
concepts.pearl: Separate sensation, interpretation, distress and disability. They interact, but they are not the same variable.

quiz.question: Which component is best described as: Detect mechanical, thermal and tissue-threat signals?
options: Peripheral receptors
Dorsal columns
Anterolateral system
Somatosensory thalamus
quiz.explanation: Specialised endings translate physical events into neural firing.

concepts.title: Motor System
concepts.subtitle: Turning intention into coordinated action
concepts.simple: The motor system turns goals into movement. The cortex plans and sends commands, while deep brain circuits, the cerebellum, brainstem and spinal cord continuously adjust force, timing and posture.
concepts.psych: Voluntary action emerges from interacting corticospinal, basal-ganglia, cerebellar and sensorimotor loops. Movement is not a simple output: prediction, sensory feedback, motivation and habit all shape what is selected and how it is executed.
concepts.advanced: Premotor and supplementary motor regions organise action plans; primary motor cortex contributes descending commands through corticobulbar and corticospinal pathways. Basal-ganglia loops bias action selection, cerebellar circuits minimise prediction error, and spinal interneuronal networks transform descending drive into coordinated muscle synergies.
concepts.analogy: A film set: the director chooses the scene, assistant directors sequence it, the camera crew makes constant corrections, and the stage machinery carries out the final movement.
concepts.care: Psychomotor slowing, agitation, tic disorders, functional movement symptoms and medication-induced motor effects require attention to both neural circuitry and behavioural context.
concepts.wrong: Damage at different levels can produce weakness, spasticity, ataxia, bradykinesia, apraxia or poorly timed movement. Similar-looking symptoms can arise from very different mechanisms.
concepts.pearl: Movement quality is a network readout: selection, prediction, sensory feedback and execution can fail independently.

quiz.question: Which structure is most associated with online prediction-error correction?
options: Cerebellum
Amygdala
Hippocampus
Hypothalamus
quiz.explanation: The cerebellum compares expected and actual movement outcomes and updates commands.

concepts.title: Autonomic Nervous System
concepts.subtitle: Regulating the body beneath awareness
concepts.simple: The autonomic nervous system quietly regulates heart rate, breathing, digestion, temperature and many other body functions. It changes state to meet demand and then helps the body recover.
concepts.psych: Sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric systems operate through central autonomic networks rather than as a simple on/off pair. Interoceptive signals, context, learning and appraisal shape bodily arousal and its conscious interpretation.
concepts.advanced: The hypothalamus, insula, anterior cingulate, amygdala, periaqueductal grey, nucleus tractus solitarius and ventrolateral medulla coordinate autonomic output. Preganglionic sympathetic neurons arise from thoracolumbar cord; parasympathetic output arises from brainstem nuclei and sacral cord. Baroreflex and chemoreflex loops stabilise internal state.
concepts.analogy: A building-management system that adjusts power, ventilation, temperature and emergency settings without waiting for the occupants to issue conscious instructions.
concepts.care: Panic, trauma-related hyperarousal, dissociation and somatic symptom presentations involve real state regulation, but no single autonomic pattern uniquely identifies a diagnosis or emotional truth.
concepts.wrong: Dysautonomia, medication effects, dehydration, endocrine illness and prolonged stress can produce palpitations, dizziness, sweating, gastrointestinal change and fatigue.
concepts.pearl: Arousal is data, not a verdict: autonomic activation signals demand, but context determines its psychological meaning.

quiz.question: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons arise primarily from the:
options: Thoracolumbar spinal cord
Occipital cortex
Sacral cortex
Cerebellar vermis
quiz.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons originate in thoracic and upper lumbar spinal segments.

concepts.title: Memory Systems
concepts.subtitle: Encoding, stabilising and retrieving experience
concepts.simple: Memory is not one storage box. Different systems hold facts, personal events, skills and short-term information, and each depends on partly different brain networks.
concepts.psych: Working memory, episodic memory, semantic knowledge, procedural learning and emotional learning are dissociable but interactive. Attention and encoding quality strongly affect what can later be retrieved.
concepts.advanced: Medial temporal structures bind distributed cortical features into relational episodic representations. Neocortical systems support semantic knowledge; frontoparietal circuits maintain task-relevant information; striatal and cerebellar systems support habits and skills. Consolidation involves synaptic change and systems-level reorganisation across time and sleep.
concepts.analogy: A library with a reception desk, temporary worktable, catalogues, archives and a workshop for learned procedures—different failures create different forms of forgetting.
concepts.care: Subjective memory complaints may reflect encoding, attention, mood, sleep, medication or retrieval difficulty rather than storage loss. Assessment must separate these mechanisms.
concepts.wrong: Hippocampal injury can impair new episodic learning; frontal dysfunction can disrupt strategy and retrieval; basal-ganglia or cerebellar disease can impair procedural learning.
concepts.pearl: Before concluding that memory was lost, ask whether the information was adequately attended to and encoded in the first place.

quiz.question: The hippocampus is especially important for:
options: Binding relational episodic details
Producing muscle force
Detecting sound frequency
Maintaining blood pressure
quiz.explanation: The hippocampal formation links distributed features into context-rich episodic representations.

concepts.title: Language Networks
concepts.subtitle: Transforming sound, symbols and meaning
concepts.simple: Language depends on networks that connect sounds, words, meanings and speech movements. There is no single “language spot”; understanding and speaking require coordinated pathways.
concepts.psych: A left-lateralised perisylvian network is common, but language organisation varies across people and tasks. Dorsal pathways support sound-to-articulation mapping; ventral pathways support sound-to-meaning mapping.
concepts.advanced: Posterior temporal cortex analyses speech and lexical-semantic information; inferior frontal and premotor systems support controlled selection, sequencing and articulation. Dorsal arcuate/superior longitudinal pathways link auditory representations to motor plans, while ventral extreme-capsule and temporal pathways support semantic processing. Right-hemisphere systems contribute prosody, discourse and pragmatic inference.
concepts.analogy: A live translation studio: one team decodes the signal, another retrieves meaning, another builds grammar, and a production crew turns the plan into speech.
concepts.care: Word-finding difficulty, slowed processing, social-pragmatic differences and language-learning history can look similar in conversation but arise from distinct mechanisms.
concepts.wrong: Network damage may produce aphasia, alexia, agraphia, apraxia of speech or impaired prosody. Symptoms depend on lesion distribution, not a rigid Broca-versus-Wernicke dichotomy.
concepts.pearl: Describe the impaired operation—comprehension, naming, repetition, grammar, motor planning or pragmatics—before assigning a localisation label.

quiz.question: The dorsal language pathway is especially involved in:
options: Sound-to-articulation mapping and repetition
Temperature regulation
Reward valuation
Visual field detection
quiz.explanation: Dorsal frontotemporal pathways support phonological sensorimotor mapping and repetition.

concepts.title: Executive Function
concepts.subtitle: Maintaining goals, adapting and regulating action
concepts.simple: Executive functions help you hold a goal in mind, resist distractions, switch strategy and check whether what you are doing is working.
concepts.psych: Executive control is a family of partly separable processes—including inhibition, working-memory updating, shifting, planning and monitoring—supported by frontoparietal, cingulo-opercular, salience and subcortical systems.
concepts.advanced: Lateral prefrontal cortex maintains abstract task rules; parietal cortex represents priorities and action-relevant information; dorsal anterior cingulate tracks conflict, effort and outcome; basal-ganglia gating regulates what enters working memory. Control is state-dependent and constrained by arousal, reward, fatigue and learned habits.
concepts.analogy: An air-traffic controller who keeps the destination active, prioritises competing demands, changes routes when conditions shift and notices when the plan is failing.
concepts.care: Executive difficulty is transdiagnostic. ADHD, depression, anxiety, trauma, sleep loss, pain and neurological illness may impair performance through different combinations of capacity, motivation and state regulation.
concepts.wrong: Frontal-network injury can cause disorganisation, impulsivity, rigidity, poor monitoring or reduced initiation, but normal structured testing does not rule out real-world executive dysfunction.
concepts.pearl: Executive performance is not a fixed trait; it reflects capacity multiplied by context, scaffolding, motivation and physiological state.

quiz.question: Executive function is best understood as:
options: A family of interacting control processes
A single ability located in one frontal spot
General intelligence only
Motor speed only
quiz.explanation: Executive control includes separable but interacting processes distributed across networks.

concepts.title: Emotion Regulation Networks
concepts.subtitle: How the brain shapes, updates and modulates emotional responses
concepts.simple: Emotion regulation is not about switching feelings off. It is the brain’s ability to notice what matters, interpret it, choose a response and recover when the situation changes.
concepts.psych: Emotion regulation emerges from coordinated activity across salience, limbic, prefrontal, hippocampal and autonomic systems. Strategies such as reappraisal, attentional deployment and response modulation recruit partly overlapping but distinct circuits.
concepts.advanced: The amygdala detects biologically and socially relevant cues; hippocampal systems supply context; anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate represent salience and internal state; ventromedial and lateral prefrontal regions update value and implement control. Regulation is bidirectional: cortical systems can modify limbic responses, while arousal and interoceptive signals constrain available control. Effective regulation therefore depends on timing, context, learning history and physiological state rather than on top-down suppression alone.
concepts.analogy: A skilled emergency coordinator: first detect what matters, check the context, choose the least costly response, then stand down when the danger has passed.
concepts.care: Clients who appear “overreactive” may be responding to rapid threat detection, weak contextual updating, limited strategy access, chronic arousal or invalidating environments. Treatment should identify the failing operation rather than moralise the behaviour.
concepts.wrong: Dysregulation can appear as impulsive escalation, prolonged rumination, emotional numbing, avoidance, dissociation or slow recovery. Similar presentations may arise from trauma, mood disorders, neurodevelopmental conditions, sleep loss, pain or substance effects.
concepts.pearl: The goal is flexible, context-sensitive responding—not feeling less. A regulated nervous system can still produce intense emotion when the situation warrants it.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes emotion regulation?
options: Flexible shaping of emotional responses across time
Suppressing all negative feelings
Using logic to eliminate emotion
A single prefrontal function
quiz.explanation: Regulation is a flexible, distributed process that changes attention, meaning, action and recovery.

concepts.title: Reward System
concepts.subtitle: Learning what to pursue, repeat and value
concepts.simple: The reward system helps the brain learn what is worth doing again. It tracks outcomes, motivation and surprise—not just pleasure.
concepts.psych: Reward processing depends on mesocorticolimbic dopamine, ventral striatum, orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus and habenular systems. Dopamine is especially important for prediction error, incentive salience and action vigour.
concepts.advanced: Midbrain dopamine neurons encode differences between expected and obtained outcomes, allowing corticostriatal circuits to update value estimates. Ventral striatum integrates reward predictions with motivational state; orbitofrontal cortex represents outcome-specific value; dorsal striatum supports learned action policies and habits. Reward behaviour is therefore shaped by learning, uncertainty, effort cost, delay, deprivation and cue exposure rather than by hedonic pleasure alone.
concepts.analogy: A learning accountant that compares the expected return with the actual return, then updates which options deserve attention and effort next time.
concepts.care: Reduced reward responsiveness can contribute to anhedonia and low initiation; exaggerated cue salience can drive compulsive behaviour; inconsistent reinforcement can make attention and persistence highly context-dependent.
concepts.wrong: Disruption may appear as apathy, impulsive choice, addiction, compulsive checking, gambling, reduced learning from consequences or rigid habits. These patterns are not explained by “low willpower” alone.
concepts.pearl: Dopamine is better understood as a teaching and energising signal than as a simple pleasure chemical.

quiz.question: Dopamine is most accurately described as:
options: A teaching and motivational signal
A pure pleasure chemical
A stress hormone only
A sensory neurotransmitter only
quiz.explanation: Dopamine supports prediction error, incentive salience and action vigour.
