concepts.title: Sleep & Circadian Rhythms
concepts.subtitle: Coordinating restoration, memory and daily biological timing
concepts.simple: Sleep is an active brain state. A daily body clock helps decide when sleep should occur, while sleep pressure builds the longer you stay awake.
concepts.psych: Sleep timing reflects interaction between circadian phase and homeostatic sleep pressure. The suprachiasmatic nucleus synchronises daily rhythms to light, while distributed brainstem, hypothalamic and thalamocortical systems generate wake, NREM and REM states.
concepts.advanced: Retinal melanopsin pathways entrain the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which coordinates endocrine, temperature and behavioural rhythms. Adenosine-related homeostatic pressure accumulates across wakefulness. VLPO sleep-promoting neurons inhibit ascending arousal systems, while orexin stabilises wakefulness. NREM slow waves and spindles support synaptic and memory processes; REM involves pontine activation, cortical desynchronisation and muscle atonia. Sleep architecture changes with age, medication, stress and illness.
concepts.analogy: Two linked controllers: a clock opens the biological sleep window, while an hourglass measures how much sleep pressure has accumulated.
concepts.care: Sleep loss can mimic or worsen inattention, emotional dysregulation, memory problems, pain sensitivity and mood symptoms. Assessment should consider timing, duration, regularity, breathing, movement, substances and medication.
concepts.wrong: Disturbance may involve insomnia, circadian delay, sleep apnoea, parasomnias, hypersomnolence or fragmented sleep. Treating “poor sleep” as one problem misses different mechanisms.
concepts.pearl: Ask when the person can sleep, not only whether they can sleep. Circadian misalignment and insomnia require different formulations.

quiz.question: Sleep timing is governed mainly by interaction between:
options: Circadian phase and homeostatic pressure
Vision and hearing
Language and memory
Motor and sensory cortex
quiz.explanation: The two-process model combines circadian timing with accumulated sleep pressure.

concepts.title: Pain Processing
concepts.subtitle: How threat, sensation, meaning and prediction become pain
concepts.simple: Pain is a protective experience created by the nervous system. It uses information from the body, but it is also shaped by attention, expectation, emotion and context.
concepts.psych: Nociception is neural encoding of potentially harmful stimuli; pain is the conscious experience. Ascending spinal and brainstem pathways interact with thalamic, insular, cingulate, somatosensory, limbic and prefrontal systems, while descending pathways can amplify or inhibit transmission.
concepts.advanced: Peripheral nociceptors signal tissue threat through Aδ and C fibres to dorsal horn circuits. Spinothalamic and spinoreticular pathways distribute information to sensory-discriminative, affective-motivational and arousal systems. Periaqueductal grey, rostroventral medulla and cortical networks provide descending modulation. In persistent pain, peripheral sensitisation, central sensitisation, altered prediction and learning can maintain pain after tissue healing, without implying that the pain is imaginary.
concepts.analogy: A security system whose sensitivity changes with recent alarms, expectations and perceived consequences—not a simple damage meter.
concepts.care: Pain intensity does not map linearly onto tissue damage. Psychological assessment should validate the experience while examining sleep, fear, avoidance, mood, attention, trauma, beliefs, medication and functional reinforcement.
concepts.wrong: Persistent pain can involve hyperalgesia, allodynia, sensitisation, reduced descending inhibition and threat-generalised avoidance. Dismissing pain as “psychological” is both inaccurate and clinically harmful.
concepts.pearl: Pain is real even when ongoing tissue damage is absent. The clinically useful question is what mechanisms are sustaining protection now.

quiz.question: Nociception refers to:
options: Neural encoding of potentially harmful stimuli
The full conscious pain experience
Fear of movement only
Tissue damage itself
quiz.explanation: Nociception is neural threat signalling; pain is the conscious protective experience.

concepts.title: Brain Health & Ageing
concepts.subtitle: Maintaining function across the lifespan
concepts.simple: Brains change throughout life. Some slowing is expected with age, but learning, movement, sleep, social connection and vascular health help protect function.
concepts.psych: Healthy ageing reflects both biological change and accumulated reserve. Processing speed, sensory efficiency and some forms of novel learning often decline, while vocabulary, expertise and emotional knowledge may remain stable or improve. Vascular, metabolic, sleep and psychosocial factors strongly influence trajectories.
concepts.advanced: Ageing involves heterogeneous changes in synaptic density, white-matter integrity, neuromodulation, vascular function and network segregation. Cognitive reserve and brain maintenance moderate clinical expression of pathology. Aerobic activity, blood-pressure control, diabetes management, hearing treatment, sleep, education and social engagement are associated with lower dementia risk, although no single intervention guarantees prevention.
concepts.analogy: An evolving transport network: routes may slow and require more maintenance, but experience, redundancy and good infrastructure can preserve effective travel.
concepts.care: Clinicians must distinguish expected age-related change from delirium, depression, medication effects, sensory loss, sleep disturbance, mild cognitive impairment and dementia. Functional decline and within-person change matter more than age stereotypes.
concepts.wrong: Pathological decline may involve progressive memory loss, executive dysfunction, language change, visuospatial problems or altered behaviour. Acute fluctuation suggests delirium and requires urgent medical assessment.
concepts.pearl: Age is a risk factor, not a diagnosis. Compare the person with their own prior functioning, not with a caricature of “normal ageing.”

quiz.question: Healthy cognitive ageing commonly involves:
options: Some slowing with preserved knowledge and expertise
Uniform severe memory loss
No variability between people
Inevitable dementia
quiz.explanation: Ageing is heterogeneous; processing speed may decline while accumulated knowledge remains strong.

concepts.title: Consciousness & Arousal
concepts.subtitle: Maintaining wakefulness, awareness and responsive engagement
concepts.simple: Consciousness depends on two linked ingredients: being awake enough to respond and having organised awareness of yourself and the world. A person can lose one more than the other.
concepts.psych: Arousal is supported by distributed brainstem, hypothalamic, thalamic and basal-forebrain systems. Conscious content depends on coordinated thalamocortical and corticocortical activity, especially across frontoparietal and sensory association networks.
concepts.advanced: The ascending arousal system uses cholinergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic, dopaminergic and histaminergic projections to stabilise wakefulness. Thalamocortical loops regulate access and integration, while posterior cortical and frontoparietal systems contribute differentiated conscious content, report and goal-directed control. Consciousness is therefore a dynamic systems property rather than a single anatomical centre.
concepts.analogy: A theatre needs the building powered and the stage lights on before a coherent performance can appear. Arousal supplies the power; distributed networks organise the scene.
concepts.care: Reduced engagement may reflect impaired arousal, delirium, dissociation, medication, sleep deprivation, depression or neurological injury. Behavioural observation alone can underestimate residual awareness.
concepts.wrong: Diffuse brain injury, bilateral thalamic damage, brainstem lesions, seizures, metabolic disturbance and sedating drugs can disrupt wakefulness or awareness. Disorders of consciousness require careful repeated assessment.
concepts.pearl: Never treat “awake” and “aware” as synonyms. Separate arousal, awareness, attention, communication and motor output.

quiz.question: Consciousness is best separated into:
options: Arousal and awareness
Memory and intelligence
Vision and hearing
Speech and movement
quiz.explanation: Arousal and awareness can dissociate clinically.

concepts.title: Brain Lateralisation
concepts.subtitle: Specialisation across two deeply connected hemispheres
concepts.simple: The two hemispheres are not duplicate brains, but they are not “logical versus creative” personalities either. They share most tasks while showing useful differences in emphasis.
concepts.psych: Language is commonly left-lateralised, while right-hemisphere systems often contribute visuospatial attention, prosody and broad contextual integration. Lateralisation varies across people, development and task demands.
concepts.advanced: Hemispheric asymmetry reflects differences in cytoarchitecture, connectivity, temporal processing and network weighting. The corpus callosum supports transfer and complementary coordination. Strong population-level tendencies do not justify inferring an individual cognitive style or diagnosis from handedness or preference.
concepts.analogy: A two-person specialist team: each partner may lead different parts of the job, but nearly every meaningful task depends on rapid communication between them.
concepts.care: Aphasia, neglect, aprosodia and split-brain findings demonstrate lateralised vulnerability, but oversimplified left-brain/right-brain labels distort formulation and psychoeducation.
concepts.wrong: Left perisylvian injury may impair language; right frontoparietal injury may produce spatial neglect or impaired prosody. Callosal disruption can impair interhemispheric transfer.
concepts.pearl: Use lateralisation as a probability statement, not a personality test.

quiz.question: The best summary of hemispheric lateralisation is:
options: Relative specialisation within an integrated system
Two independent personalities
Left equals logic and right equals creativity
Only the dominant hemisphere matters
quiz.explanation: Lateralisation concerns probabilistic functional weighting within connected networks.

concepts.title: Neuroimmunology
concepts.subtitle: How immune signalling shapes brain function and behaviour
concepts.simple: The brain and immune system constantly exchange information. Immune signals can protect and repair tissue, but prolonged or misdirected inflammation can also change energy, mood, thinking and pain.
concepts.psych: Microglia, astrocytes, endothelial cells, peripheral immune cells and cytokines influence synaptic plasticity, sickness behaviour and stress responsivity. Neuroimmune effects are context-dependent and not equivalent to “inflammation causes every symptom.”
concepts.advanced: Pattern-recognition receptors detect injury and pathogens, activating cytokine, complement and inflammasome pathways. Microglia can support pruning, trophic signalling and repair or contribute to synaptic dysfunction when activation is persistent. Blood–brain barrier dynamics, vagal signalling and humoral routes couple peripheral immune state to central networks.
concepts.analogy: A security and maintenance service: it patrols, clears debris and coordinates repair, but a prolonged alarm can disrupt normal work throughout the building.
concepts.care: Fatigue, anhedonia, psychomotor slowing and cognitive fog can accompany immune activation, but these symptoms remain nonspecific. Clinical reasoning must integrate medical, psychological and contextual evidence.
concepts.wrong: Infection, autoimmune disease, traumatic injury and chronic inflammatory states can alter neural function. Rarely, autoimmune encephalitis can present with acute psychiatric and neurological symptoms.
concepts.pearl: Neuroinflammation is a mechanism, not a diagnosis—and “activated” immune cells are not automatically harmful.

quiz.question: Microglia are best described as:
options: Resident immune-surveillance cells of the CNS
Peripheral motor neurons
Endocrine glands
Myelin-forming cells in the PNS
quiz.explanation: Microglia are CNS-resident immune cells with surveillance, pruning and repair roles.

concepts.title: Brain Energy Metabolism
concepts.subtitle: Fuel, oxygen and the energetic cost of neural computation
concepts.simple: The brain is small compared with the body but expensive to run. Neurons need a steady supply of oxygen and glucose to maintain ion gradients, communicate and repair themselves.
concepts.psych: Neural activity couples to local blood flow and metabolism. Astrocytes, neurons, mitochondria and cerebral vessels coordinate substrate delivery, ATP production and waste handling.
concepts.advanced: Most ATP supports ion pumping and synaptic signalling. Oxidative phosphorylation supplies high-yield energy, while glycolysis and lactate shuttling contribute dynamically according to cell type and demand. Neurovascular coupling links activity to perfusion; hypoglycaemia, hypoxia or mitochondrial dysfunction rapidly impair cognition and consciousness.
concepts.analogy: A high-performance data centre: computation is only possible when power, cooling, fuel delivery and waste removal remain tightly matched to demand.
concepts.care: Fatigue, slowed thinking and poor concentration can arise from sleep, mood, medication, endocrine, vascular, respiratory or metabolic factors. Symptoms alone do not identify the mechanism.
concepts.wrong: Hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, stroke, seizures and mitochondrial disease can cause rapid functional failure. Chronic vascular and metabolic burden can gradually reduce network efficiency.
concepts.pearl: The brain stores little fuel. Continuous supply and precise regulation matter more than simple “brain energy” slogans.

quiz.question: Most neural ATP is used substantially for:
options: Maintaining and restoring ion gradients
Growing hair
Producing cerebrospinal fluid only
Storing long-term glucose
quiz.explanation: Ion pumping and synaptic signalling dominate the energy budget.

concepts.title: Integrated Systems Capstone
concepts.subtitle: Reasoning from cells to circuits, behaviour and clinical presentation
concepts.simple: A real behaviour never comes from one brain part. It emerges from cells, circuits, body state, learning and context working together over time.
concepts.psych: Clinical neuroscience is strongest when it links levels of explanation without collapsing one into another. Symptoms should be formulated across cellular, network, cognitive, behavioural, interpersonal and environmental processes.
concepts.advanced: Multilevel causal models distinguish mechanism, mediator, moderator and marker. Neural findings constrain hypotheses but rarely determine diagnosis alone. Robust formulation integrates time course, state dependence, development, compensation, measurement limits and alternative explanations.
concepts.analogy: A traffic problem can involve one broken signal, road design, weather, driver behaviour and peak-hour demand. Looking at only one layer gives an incomplete answer.
concepts.care: Neurobiological explanations can reduce blame, but they can also become deterministic or falsely precise. Clinical usefulness depends on whether the model improves assessment, intervention or communication.
concepts.wrong: Reductionism may over-localise symptoms, mistake correlation for cause or ignore context. Purely psychosocial accounts can also miss neurological, medical or medication contributors.
concepts.pearl: The best formulation is not the most biological one; it is the model that explains the pattern, survives alternatives and guides safe action.

quiz.question: A multilevel formulation should:
options: Link biological, cognitive, behavioural and contextual processes
Replace psychology with anatomy
Assume one cause per symptom
Ignore alternative explanations
quiz.explanation: Clinical phenomena usually require linked levels of explanation.

concepts.title: Personality Disorders: Network and Developmental Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Stable patterns emerge from development, learning, temperament and context—not a single “personality centre”
concepts.simple: Personality is the brain’s long-term way of predicting people, regulating emotion and choosing how to respond. Personality disorder patterns can develop when these strategies become rigid, costly and difficult to update across situations.
concepts.psych: Personality pathology is best understood as dimensional dysfunction in self and interpersonal functioning, interacting with maladaptive trait domains. Neurobiological findings implicate distributed systems for salience, threat, reward, mentalising, autobiographical self-processing and cognitive control, but no scan diagnoses a personality disorder.
concepts.advanced: Research describes heterogeneous alterations in frontolimbic reactivity, connectivity and learning across diagnostic groups, with substantial overlap with trauma exposure, mood disorders, neurodevelopmental conditions and substance use. Developmental models emphasise gene–environment interplay, attachment learning, reinforcement history, social cognition and state-dependent network dynamics. Group-level neural differences are not sufficiently specific for individual diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: A navigation system trained on years of journeys: it can become excellent at avoiding familiar danger, yet repeatedly choose the same detour even when the road has changed.
concepts.care: A neuroscience-informed formulation can reduce moral judgement while preserving accountability. Treatment targets modifiable processes—emotion regulation, mentalising, behavioural flexibility, interpersonal learning and distress tolerance—rather than treating personality as biologically fixed.
concepts.wrong: Rigid threat predictions, unstable self-representation, impulsive reinforcement learning, interpersonal hypersensitivity or reduced behavioural flexibility can perpetuate crises and relational disruption. Similar patterns may reflect trauma, autism, ADHD, mood states, psychosis, substance effects or environmental danger and require careful differential assessment.
concepts.pearl: Biology may help explain vulnerability; it never excuses harm or makes change impossible. Formulate functions and learning histories, not “bad brain regions.”

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects current neuroscience of personality disorders?
options: They involve heterogeneous distributed processes shaped by development and learning
A single abnormal brain region confirms the diagnosis
Brain imaging can reliably distinguish every personality disorder in one person
Personality patterns are biologically fixed and cannot change
quiz.explanation: Findings are distributed, overlapping and probabilistic; diagnosis remains clinical and change remains possible.

concepts.title: Sleep Disorders Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: When circadian timing, sleep pressure, arousal or breathing disrupt restorative sleep
concepts.simple: Sleep is controlled by a body clock, growing sleep pressure and brain systems that switch between waking and sleep. Sleep disorders happen when timing, breathing, movement, arousal or sleep regulation repeatedly interferes with this process.
concepts.psych: Insomnia involves persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep with daytime consequences and often includes conditioned arousal, threat monitoring and maladaptive sleep effort. Obstructive sleep apnoea produces repeated airway collapse, hypoxia and fragmentation. Circadian rhythm disorders reflect misalignment between internal timing and required schedules. Parasomnias and central hypersomnolence disorders involve distinct state-control mechanisms.
concepts.advanced: Sleep–wake regulation emerges from interaction between circadian signals from the suprachiasmatic nucleus, homeostatic sleep pressure, hypothalamic sleep-promoting neurons, ascending arousal systems and orexin-mediated state stability. Disorder mechanisms differ: hyperarousal and learned associations in insomnia; upper-airway obstruction and autonomic surges in OSA; phase misalignment in circadian disorders; REM/NREM state dissociation in parasomnias.
concepts.analogy: A theatre with a timetable, dimmer switch and security system: sleep fails when the schedule is wrong, the lights cannot dim, alarms keep firing or airflow to the building is repeatedly blocked.
concepts.care: Poor sleep can mimic or amplify inattention, low mood, irritability, memory difficulty, pain and emotion dysregulation. Psychological assessment should screen timing, duration, regularity, snoring, witnessed apnoeas, restless legs, substances, medication and daytime sleepiness.
concepts.wrong: Chronic insomnia can perpetuate distress and functional impairment; untreated OSA increases cardiovascular and cognitive risk; severe sleep deprivation may worsen mania, psychosis, seizures and suicidality. Red flags include dangerous sleepiness, nocturnal breathing pauses, cataplexy or injurious parasomnias.
concepts.pearl: “I sleep badly” is a symptom, not a mechanism. Separate insomnia, circadian misalignment, breathing disturbance, movement and hypersomnolence before choosing treatment.

quiz.question: Which system most directly provides the brain’s central circadian timing signal?
options: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
Amygdala
Primary motor cortex
Caudate nucleus
quiz.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus coordinates circadian timing using retinal light input and downstream signals.

concepts.title: Substance Use and Addiction Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Reward learning, adaptation, stress and control across repeated substance exposure
concepts.simple: Addictive substances can strongly teach the brain that a drug and its cues matter. Over time, wanting, habit and withdrawal can grow even when pleasure falls and consequences become severe.
concepts.psych: Substance use disorders involve impaired control, salience, risky use and physiological adaptation. Repeated exposure recruits reward, habit, stress, memory and executive-control systems. Learning becomes cue-bound and state-dependent; negative reinforcement increasingly sustains use by relieving withdrawal or distress.
concepts.advanced: Drugs differ pharmacologically but can converge on mesocorticolimbic dopamine and downstream plasticity. Incentive sensitisation may amplify cue-triggered wanting; allostatic adaptation shifts hedonic set points; dorsal striatal recruitment supports habitual responding; prefrontal and interoceptive networks influence choice and relapse. These models are complementary, not universal explanations for every person.
concepts.analogy: A learning algorithm whose priority weights are repeatedly overwritten: cues linked to the substance become bright, urgent shortcuts while delayed costs are discounted.
concepts.care: A non-moralising model supports motivational interviewing, contingency management, relapse prevention and medication where indicated. Assessment must include intoxication, withdrawal risk, polysubstance use, overdose, driving, pregnancy, medical complications and social context.
concepts.wrong: Tolerance, withdrawal, overdose, seizures, psychosis, mood destabilisation, cognitive impairment and interpersonal harm vary by substance and pattern. Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can be medically dangerous; opioid overdose can suppress breathing.
concepts.pearl: Dopamine is not simply pleasure. It helps update motivational significance and learning. Addiction is neither pure choice nor loss of all agency—it is constrained, learned behaviour that can change with effective support.

quiz.question: Negative reinforcement in substance use means:
options: Use increases because it removes or reduces an aversive state
Use is punished immediately
The substance has no learned effects
Dopamine permanently eliminates choice
quiz.explanation: Relief of withdrawal, anxiety or distress can strengthen future use.

concepts.title: Neurodegenerative Disorders
concepts.subtitle: Progressive cellular vulnerability expressed through distinct network syndromes
concepts.simple: Neurodegenerative disorders gradually damage particular brain cells and networks. The pattern matters: memory may change first in one disorder, movement in another, and language or behaviour in another.
concepts.psych: Alzheimer disease, Lewy body disease, frontotemporal degeneration, Parkinson disease and related conditions have overlapping but distinguishable cognitive, behavioural, motor and psychiatric profiles. Symptoms emerge from network degeneration, neurotransmitter changes, protein pathology and loss of compensation—not normal ageing alone.
concepts.advanced: Protein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, synaptic failure and selective cellular vulnerability interact differently across diseases. Amyloid-β and tau are central to Alzheimer pathophysiology; α-synuclein to Parkinson/Lewy body disorders; tau or TDP-43 to many frontotemporal degenerations. Biomarkers support diagnosis but must be interpreted within phenotype and stage.
concepts.analogy: A transport network losing specific stations and lines over time: early symptoms depend on which route is affected, while later disruption spreads across connected systems.
concepts.care: Psychologists contribute through cognitive assessment, behavioural formulation, capacity evaluation, caregiver support and adaptation of interventions. Depression, delirium, medication effects, sleep disorders and sensory loss can mimic or worsen decline and must be assessed.
concepts.wrong: Progressive memory loss, visuospatial errors, fluctuations, hallucinations, parkinsonism, disinhibition, language decline or loss of daily function may signal disease-specific syndromes. Sudden decline is not typical degeneration and requires urgent evaluation for delirium, stroke or other acute causes.
concepts.pearl: “Dementia” describes functional impact, not one disease. Diagnose the syndrome, consider the cause, and always establish time course.

quiz.question: Which feature most strongly argues against uncomplicated neurodegeneration as the sole cause?
options: Abrupt onset over hours
Gradual progression over years
Increasing difficulty with instrumental activities
A reproducible cognitive profile
quiz.explanation: Abrupt change suggests delirium, stroke, seizure, medication effect or another acute process.

concepts.title: Epilepsy Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Pathological network synchrony, seizure propagation and the cognitive–psychological context
concepts.simple: A seizure is a temporary burst of abnormal, overly synchronised brain activity. Epilepsy means there is an enduring tendency for unprovoked seizures—not every faint, stare or convulsion is epilepsy.
concepts.psych: Seizures are classified by onset and clinical features. Focal seizures begin in networks within one hemisphere and may affect awareness, sensation, emotion, memory or movement; generalised seizures rapidly engage bilateral networks. Cognition and mental health are shaped by aetiology, seizure burden, sleep, medication, stigma and psychosocial restriction.
concepts.advanced: Epileptogenesis reflects altered excitation–inhibition balance, ion-channel function, synaptic organisation, gliosis and network connectivity. Seizure initiation and spread depend on local circuitry and large-scale propagation pathways. Interictal discharges can disrupt processing transiently. EEG supports classification but a normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy, and incidental abnormalities do not establish diagnosis without clinical correlation.
concepts.analogy: A stadium where a local chant can remain contained or rapidly recruit the whole crowd. The important questions are where it begins, how it spreads and what the network does before and after.
concepts.care: Psychologists may encounter memory complaints, anxiety, depression, trauma after seizures, functional/dissociative seizures and medication effects. Distinguishing epileptic from functional seizures requires specialist assessment; both are real and may coexist.
concepts.wrong: Prolonged seizures, repeated seizures without recovery, injury, pregnancy or first seizure require urgent medical evaluation. Sudden unexplained death in epilepsy is uncommon but clinically important; adherence, nocturnal supervision discussions and seizure control matter.
concepts.pearl: Epilepsy is a network disorder, not simply “too much electricity.” Do not diagnose seizure type from appearance alone, and do not equate functional seizures with faking.

quiz.question: Which statement about routine EEG is correct?
options: A normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy
A normal EEG proves events are psychological
Any sharp wave confirms epilepsy regardless of history
EEG identifies every seizure type with certainty
quiz.explanation: Routine EEG has limited sensitivity and must be interpreted with the clinical history.

concepts.title: Traumatic Brain Injury Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Mechanical forces, network disruption and recovery across time
concepts.simple: A traumatic brain injury happens when an external force disrupts how the brain works. Some effects are immediate, while others emerge as the brain responds to injury, inflammation, fatigue and altered network efficiency.
concepts.psych: TBI ranges from mild concussion to severe injury. Symptoms may involve attention, processing speed, memory, emotion regulation, sleep, headache and sensory tolerance. Outcome reflects injury severity, premorbid functioning, repeated injury, psychosocial context and recovery expectations—not scan findings alone.
concepts.advanced: Primary injury includes focal contusion, haemorrhage, axonal stretch and vascular disruption. Secondary cascades involve excitotoxicity, ionic imbalance, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation and altered cerebral metabolism. Diffuse axonal injury preferentially affects long white-matter pathways and can produce disconnection without a large focal lesion. Persistent symptoms after mild TBI are multifactorial and may be maintained by sleep disturbance, pain, vestibular dysfunction, threat appraisal, mood and deconditioning.
concepts.analogy: A city shaken by an earthquake: some roads are visibly damaged, while other routes look intact but transmit traffic inefficiently until repairs and rerouting occur.
concepts.care: Psychologists help distinguish acute post-concussive change from depression, PTSD, pain, sleep disorder, medication effects and functional amplification. Graded return to activity, pacing and expectation management are usually more helpful than prolonged total rest.
concepts.wrong: Red flags include deteriorating consciousness, repeated vomiting, seizure, focal weakness, worsening severe headache, unequal pupils or new confusion. Repeated injuries can increase risk and warrant careful return-to-play or work decisions.
concepts.pearl: Symptoms after mild TBI are real, but persistent difficulty is rarely explained by one damaged brain region. Recovery is biological, cognitive and contextual.
concepts.learnMore: Review the mechanism map, clinical cautions and source list in the concept detail panel.

quiz.question: Diffuse axonal injury primarily involves:
options: Stretching and disruption of long white-matter axons
Only skull fracture
A single neurotransmitter deficiency
Voluntary symptom production

concepts.title: Migraine Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: A sensory-processing and trigeminovascular brain disorder
concepts.simple: Migraine is more than a bad headache. It is a brain disorder that can change sensory sensitivity, attention, nausea, mood and pain before, during and after an attack.
concepts.psych: Migraine reflects altered excitability and sensory gain across brainstem, hypothalamic, thalamic and cortical systems, with activation of the trigeminovascular pathway. Attacks may include aura, photophobia, phonophobia, cognitive slowing and postdrome fatigue. Stress can trigger attacks but does not make migraine psychological.
concepts.advanced: Cortical spreading depolarisation is strongly linked to aura, while trigeminal afferents and calcitonin gene-related peptide contribute to meningeal nociceptive signalling. Hypothalamic and brainstem changes may precede pain, consistent with a cyclic state disorder rather than a purely vascular event. Central sensitisation can produce allodynia and chronification. Genetic susceptibility, sleep, hormones, sensory load and learning history influence threshold.
concepts.analogy: A sensory control room with the gain turned too high: ordinary light, sound and internal signals become amplified until the system enters an attack state.
concepts.care: Migraine can mimic panic, dissociation, cognitive disorder or neurological disease. Psychologists can support trigger pattern recognition, sleep regularity, stress regulation, pacing and reduction of medication-overuse cycles without implying the disorder is “caused by stress.”
concepts.wrong: A sudden thunderclap headache, new focal deficit, fever with neck stiffness, pregnancy-related severe headache or a major change in pattern requires urgent medical assessment.
concepts.pearl: Migraine is a disorder of brain state regulation and sensory processing, not simply dilated blood vessels.

options: Cortical spreading depolarisation
Permanent cortical necrosis
Only muscle tension
Reduced cerebrospinal fluid

concepts.title: Eating Disorders Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Interoception, reward, habit and threat in disorders of eating and body image
concepts.simple: Eating disorders change how the brain interprets hunger, reward, threat and body-related information. They are serious illnesses, not choices or vanity.
concepts.psych: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder involve different patterns of restriction, bingeing, compensatory behaviour and weight/shape overvaluation. Relevant systems include interoception, cognitive control, reward learning, habit, threat and social evaluation. Starvation itself alters cognition, emotion and reward, complicating causal interpretation.
concepts.advanced: Findings implicate insular, striatal, frontoparietal and limbic circuitry, but there is no diagnostic neural signature. Restriction may become negatively reinforcing by reducing anxiety; repeated behaviours become habitual; prediction errors around food and body cues may be distorted. Energy deficiency changes dopamine, serotonin, endocrine function and network efficiency. Weight restoration can reverse some abnormalities, while trait vulnerabilities may remain.
concepts.analogy: A navigation system whose hunger signals, danger alarms and reward maps have become miscalibrated—then further distorted by starvation and repetition.
concepts.care: Medical risk can be high at any body size. Psychologists should monitor restriction, bingeing, purging, compulsive exercise, suicidality and rapid change, while coordinating medical and nutritional care. Neurobiological framing should reduce blame, not reduce behavioural accountability or urgency.
concepts.wrong: Bradycardia, syncope, electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, haematemesis, severe weakness, acute food refusal or escalating suicidality require urgent medical review. Refeeding syndrome is a medical emergency risk in severely malnourished patients.
concepts.pearl: The starving brain cannot be interpreted as if it were metabolically neutral; state effects and trait vulnerability must be separated.
concepts.learnMore: Review the mechanism map, clinical cautions and source list in the concept detail panel.

quiz.question: A major interpretive problem in eating-disorder neuroimaging is that:
options: Starvation itself changes brain and behaviour
The brain is unaffected by nutrition
Only body weight matters
All disorders share one neural signature

concepts.title: Tic and Tourette Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Urges, inhibition and habit-like motor-vocal output
concepts.simple: Tics are sudden movements or sounds that the brain produces repeatedly. Many people feel a build-up urge before the tic and temporary relief afterwards.
concepts.psych: Tourette syndrome involves multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic over time. Tics fluctuate with arousal, attention, fatigue and context. Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, sensorimotor gating and action selection are central. Suppression is possible for some people but effortful and often followed by rebound or fatigue.
concepts.advanced: Models emphasise altered basal-ganglia inhibition, sensorimotor prediction, habit learning and heightened salience of premonitory urges. Dopaminergic modulation is relevant but insufficient as a complete explanation. Voluntary control and involuntary generation coexist: a person may consciously release a tic to relieve an involuntary urge. Comorbid ADHD, OCD and anxiety often contribute more impairment than tic frequency alone.
concepts.analogy: A notification system that repeatedly generates high-priority motor prompts; ignoring them is possible for a while, but consumes bandwidth.
concepts.care: Assessment should distinguish tics from stereotypies, compulsions, seizures, dystonia and functional tic-like behaviours. Comprehensive Behavioural Intervention for Tics uses awareness and competing responses without shaming or demanding constant suppression.
concepts.wrong: Sudden explosive onset of complex tic-like behaviour, especially with marked social modelling or atypical phenomenology, requires careful differential assessment. New neurological signs or medication-related onset need medical review.
concepts.pearl: Suppressibility does not make a tic voluntary in the ordinary sense; effortful control can coexist with involuntary urge generation.
concepts.learnMore: Review the mechanism map, clinical cautions and source list in the concept detail panel.

quiz.question: A premonitory urge is:
options: An uncomfortable sensation that may precede a tic
Proof the tic is deliberate
A type of seizure discharge
Always absent in Tourette syndrome

concepts.title: Intellectual Developmental Disability Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Developmental differences in reasoning, learning and adaptive functioning
concepts.simple: Intellectual developmental disability means a person learns and solves everyday problems more slowly and also needs support with practical, social or conceptual tasks. It is not defined by one test score alone.
concepts.psych: Diagnosis requires deficits in intellectual functions and adaptive functioning with developmental onset. Severity is based on adaptive support needs rather than IQ alone. Causes are heterogeneous and may include genetic syndromes, prenatal exposure, perinatal complications, neurological conditions or unknown factors.
concepts.advanced: There is no single neural mechanism. Diverse aetiologies can alter synaptic development, excitation–inhibition balance, white-matter organisation, cortical maturation or metabolic function. Cognitive profiles are often uneven, and test performance is influenced by language, attention, motor demands, culture, opportunity and health. Adaptive functioning integrates real-world performance across conceptual, social and practical domains.
concepts.analogy: A learning system that needs more repetitions, clearer steps and stronger environmental scaffolding—not a system that cannot learn.
concepts.care: Psychologists should assess strengths, adaptive functioning, communication, comorbid ADHD/ASD, trauma exposure, sensory needs and medical contributors. Supports should maximise autonomy and participation while avoiding both unrealistic demands and unnecessary restriction.
concepts.wrong: Diagnostic overshadowing can cause pain, depression, psychosis, abuse or medical illness to be missed. Sudden functional decline is not explained by a lifelong developmental disability and needs assessment.
concepts.pearl: IQ estimates capacity under test conditions; adaptive functioning determines how much support is needed in daily life.
concepts.learnMore: Review the mechanism map, clinical cautions and source list in the concept detail panel.

quiz.question: Severity of intellectual developmental disability is primarily based on:
options: Adaptive functioning and support needs
IQ score alone
Brain-scan appearance
School grade only

concepts.title: Learning Disorders Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Why reading, writing and mathematics can diverge from general ability
concepts.simple: Specific learning disorders happen when the brain finds one type of academic learning unusually difficult, even when teaching, opportunity and overall intelligence are adequate.
concepts.psych: Reading, written expression and mathematics depend on partially distinct distributed networks. Dyslexia commonly involves inefficient phonological processing and reduced automaticity in left temporoparietal and occipitotemporal systems. Dyscalculia often involves atypical number-magnitude representation and frontoparietal integration. Difficulties are developmental, dimensional and frequently overlap with ADHD, language disorder and developmental coordination disorder.
concepts.advanced: Neuroimaging findings are group-level and heterogeneous rather than diagnostic biomarkers. Learning emerges through experience-dependent tuning of cortical systems that were not evolutionarily specialised for literacy or formal mathematics. Risk reflects polygenic liability, language exposure, instructional history and network efficiency. Intervention can alter activation patterns, but normalisation is neither necessary nor sufficient for functional improvement.
concepts.analogy: A capable computer with one specialist program that loads slowly and needs more explicit shortcuts.
concepts.care: Assessment should test the referral question, academic skills, cognitive-linguistic contributors, educational opportunity and functional impact. The goal is to identify the learning process that is breaking down and the support that changes performance.
concepts.wrong: Do not infer laziness, low intelligence or poor parenting from slow academic progress. Sudden loss of established skills, seizures, neurological signs or broad regression require medical investigation.
concepts.pearl: A discrepancy between IQ and achievement is not required; the clinically important issue is persistent skill difficulty despite appropriate instruction.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects current evidence about dyslexia?
options: It involves inefficient development of reading-related networks and is not a marker of low intelligence
It is caused by poor motivation
It can be diagnosed from a single brain scan
It always resolves without intervention
quiz.explanation: Dyslexia reflects persistent difficulty in reading processes despite adequate opportunity and is unrelated to low intelligence.

concepts.title: Communication Disorders Neuroscience
concepts.subtitle: Language, speech and social communication across development
concepts.simple: Communication disorders occur when understanding, producing or using language and speech is much harder than expected for age.
concepts.psych: Language depends on distributed temporal, frontal, parietal, auditory and motor systems linked by dorsal and ventral white-matter pathways. Developmental language disorder may affect vocabulary, grammar, discourse or verbal learning. Speech sound disorder concerns production; childhood apraxia of speech involves impaired planning or programming of speech movements; social pragmatic difficulties affect context-sensitive use of communication.
concepts.advanced: Network development is shaped by genetic liability, auditory-linguistic exposure, motor planning and social interaction. There is no single “language centre” or diagnostic scan. Profiles are often uneven and overlap with ADHD, autism, dyslexia, hearing impairment and intellectual disability. Bilingualism does not cause language disorder; impairment should be evident across the child’s languages relative to exposure.
concepts.analogy: A communication network where messages may be understood, formulated, sequenced or socially routed at different speeds.
concepts.care: Psychologists should distinguish language competence from behaviour, attention and noncompliance. Assessment requires hearing history, developmental context, language exposure and collaboration with speech pathology.
concepts.wrong: New aphasia, facial weakness, dysarthria or abrupt speech change requires urgent neurological assessment. Persistent communication difficulty should not be attributed to bilingualism without evidence across languages.
concepts.pearl: A child who cannot formulate language efficiently may look inattentive, oppositional or socially awkward when the primary bottleneck is communication.

quiz.question: Bilingualism and developmental language disorder are best understood as:
options: Bilingualism does not cause the disorder; difficulty should be evident relative to exposure across languages
Any second language causes delay
Only English testing is needed
Bilingual children cannot be assessed
quiz.explanation: Language disorder is not caused by bilingualism and must be judged against appropriate exposure in each language.

concepts.title: Anxiety Spectrum Comparison
concepts.subtitle: Shared threat circuitry, different predictions and avoidance patterns
concepts.simple: Anxiety disorders share an overactive alarm system, but differ in what the brain predicts is dangerous and how the person tries to stay safe.
concepts.psych: Across anxiety disorders, threat appraisal, salience detection, interoception, avoidance learning and uncertainty are central. Generalised anxiety emphasises diffuse future threat; panic disorder emphasises catastrophic interpretation of bodily sensations; social anxiety emphasises negative evaluation; specific phobia involves circumscribed cues; separation anxiety focuses on attachment-related harm. OCD is related but includes intrusive thoughts and compulsive neutralisation rather than fear alone.
concepts.advanced: Amygdala-centred accounts are insufficient. Anxiety reflects interactions among insula, anterior cingulate, hippocampus, prefrontal regulation, periaqueductal grey, autonomic systems and learning history. Avoidance prevents prediction error and maintains overestimation of danger. Effective exposure is inhibitory learning: building new safety or tolerability associations rather than erasing fear.
concepts.analogy: The same security system using different threat rules—body sensations, social judgement, uncertainty, separation or specific cues.
concepts.care: Formulation should identify feared outcomes, safety behaviours, attentional bias, avoidance and reinforcement. Treatment is more precise when exposure targets the prediction being tested.
concepts.wrong: Acute chest pain, syncope, neurological deficits, intoxication, withdrawal or endocrine disturbance can mimic anxiety and require medical consideration. Trauma, autism-related overload and psychosis also demand differential assessment.
concepts.pearl: Name the feared catastrophe, not just the symptom. “Anxiety” is the alarm; the formulation is the prediction.

quiz.question: What most clearly distinguishes anxiety presentations?
options: The predicted catastrophe and associated safety behaviour
Whether the amygdala activates
Whether distress is real
Whether symptoms occur daily
quiz.explanation: Anxiety disorders share mechanisms but differ in feared outcomes and maintaining responses.

concepts.title: Psychopharmacology Foundations
concepts.subtitle: How psychiatric medicines change signalling without reducing people to chemistry
concepts.simple: Psychiatric medicines change how brain signals are sent or regulated. They can reduce symptoms, but they do not replace learning, relationships or context.
concepts.psych: Most psychotropics alter receptor activity, transporter function, ion channels or intracellular signalling. Clinical effects emerge over different timescales and reflect downstream adaptation, not merely immediate neurotransmitter change. Antidepressants, stimulants, antipsychotics, mood stabilisers and anxiolytics have distinct benefit-risk profiles, and the same medicine can affect sleep, appetite, arousal and cognition.
concepts.advanced: Simple “chemical imbalance” explanations are misleading. Drug effects are network-level, state-dependent and probabilistic. Pharmacokinetics determines absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; pharmacodynamics concerns what the drug does at its targets. CYP interactions, half-life, active metabolites, withdrawal, adherence and placebo/nocebo processes all matter clinically. Psychological practice should support informed decision-making without prescribing outside scope.
concepts.analogy: Adjusting the gain, timing or filtering in a communication network rather than replacing a missing chemical.
concepts.care: Psychologists should understand common indications, side effects, activation, sedation, discontinuation effects and interactions so they can monitor function and communicate with prescribers.
concepts.wrong: New suicidality, severe agitation, serotonin-toxicity signs, manic activation, rigidity with fever, seizures or significant metabolic change require urgent medical review. Abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal or relapse.
concepts.pearl: Medication response is evidence about treatment effect, not proof of a diagnosis or a single underlying chemical defect.

quiz.question: Pharmacokinetics refers to:
options: What the body does to the drug over time
Only receptor binding
Whether a diagnosis is correct
The meaning a patient gives medication
quiz.explanation: Pharmacokinetics covers absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination.

concepts.title: Clinical Neuroanatomy Review
concepts.subtitle: Localisation, networks and differential reasoning in practice
concepts.simple: Clinical neuroanatomy asks which brain systems could produce a pattern of changes—and what else might explain it.
concepts.psych: Localisation begins with time course, laterality, modality and functional pattern. Focal cortical, subcortical, brainstem, cerebellar, peripheral and diffuse network syndromes produce different constellations. Modern reasoning combines lesion localisation with disconnection, diaschisis, compensation and context. A normal structural scan does not rule out functional impairment, and a lesion does not explain every symptom.
concepts.advanced: High-value reasoning moves from syndrome to anatomical hypothesis, then tests vascular territory, tract, network and differential diagnosis. Double dissociations support functional architecture, but real patients show distributed and overlapping deficits. Cognitive findings must be interpreted alongside effort, fatigue, language, mood, pain, medications, premorbid ability and ecological validity.
concepts.analogy: Troubleshooting a city by asking whether the problem lies in one building, a transport route, the power grid or city-wide conditions.
concepts.care: Psychologists use neuroanatomy to sharpen hypotheses, recognise red flags, interpret cognitive patterns and communicate uncertainty. Localisation should guide—not substitute for—medical assessment and formulation.
concepts.wrong: Acute focal deficit, thunderclap headache, new seizure, rapidly progressive cognitive change or fluctuating consciousness requires urgent medical assessment. Do not overlocalise nonspecific symptoms.
concepts.pearl: The strongest localisation comes from a coherent pattern across functions, time course and examination—not from one low test score.

quiz.question: The most reliable basis for localisation is:
options: A coherent pattern across symptoms, time course and examination
One isolated low score
A diagnosis label alone
Patient age only
quiz.explanation: Localisation is strongest when multiple converging findings form an anatomically plausible syndrome.

concepts.title: Attention in Neuropsychology
concepts.subtitle: Selecting, sustaining and shifting limited processing resources
concepts.simple: Attention is the brain’s way of choosing what gets priority. It helps you notice what matters, stay with it, ignore distractions and switch when the task changes.
concepts.psych: Attention is not one unitary skill. Clinical assessment distinguishes alertness, sustained attention, selective attention, divided attention and attentional control. Performance depends on arousal, motivation, sensory load, working memory and executive regulation.
concepts.advanced: Attention emerges from interacting dorsal and ventral attention systems, thalamic and brainstem arousal mechanisms, frontoparietal control networks and neuromodulatory systems. Test scores are highly state-sensitive: sleep, pain, anxiety, medication, effort and task novelty can alter performance without indicating a fixed attentional deficit.
concepts.analogy: A theatre spotlight controlled by a stage manager: brightness is arousal, focus is selection, and moving the beam is shifting.
concepts.care: Psychologists need to separate trait-like attentional vulnerability from situational overload, slowed processing, mood-related interference and executive dyscontrol. This distinction changes both diagnosis and intervention.
concepts.wrong: Acute inattention with fluctuating consciousness may indicate delirium. Marked change after head injury, seizure, medication change or neurological illness requires medical review.
concepts.pearl: A low attention score is a description of performance under specific conditions, not a diagnosis by itself.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive mechanism map and references below for assessment implications and evidence sources.

quiz.question: Which task best measures sustained attention?
options: Monitoring a stream of stimuli for infrequent targets
Naming pictures
Copying a design
Recalling a story
quiz.explanation: Sustained-attention tasks require maintaining readiness over time.

concepts.title: Processing Speed
concepts.subtitle: How efficiently simple cognitive operations are completed
concepts.simple: Processing speed is how quickly the brain can take in simple information, make a small decision and respond accurately. It is not the same as intelligence or rushing.
concepts.psych: Processing-speed measures sample visual scanning, graphomotor output, decision speed and sustained efficiency. Slow scores can reflect motor limitations, visual difficulty, fatigue, depression, medication effects, cautious style or broader white-matter inefficiency.
concepts.advanced: Speeded performance depends on distributed network integrity, myelination, white-matter connectivity, sensory encoding, motor output and strategic trade-offs between speed and accuracy. Processing speed is often a foundational constraint: when basic operations consume more time, working memory and executive resources become overloaded during complex tasks.
concepts.analogy: The bandwidth of a network: the information may be correct, but limited throughput creates bottlenecks when demands accumulate.
concepts.care: Psychologists should interpret speed scores alongside accuracy, motor demands, visual load and untimed reasoning. Slow speed can create real functional impairment even when reasoning is strong.
concepts.wrong: Sudden slowing, new motor changes or broad cognitive decline requires medical assessment. Longstanding slow speed may reflect neurodevelopmental variation rather than acquired disease.
concepts.pearl: Slow processing speed often changes how much a person can do in time—not what they can understand.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive mechanism map and references below for assessment implications and evidence sources.

quiz.question: Processing-speed tests usually measure:
options: Efficiency on simple, speeded tasks
Overall intelligence directly
Long-term memory storage
Personality
quiz.explanation: They assess how efficiently simple operations are completed under time pressure.

concepts.title: Working Memory
concepts.subtitle: Holding and manipulating information for immediate goals
concepts.simple: Working memory is the brain’s mental workbench. It lets you hold a small amount of information in mind while doing something with it.
concepts.psych: Working memory includes temporary maintenance and active manipulation. Verbal and visuospatial stores interact with attentional control and long-term knowledge. Performance is limited and vulnerable to distraction, stress, fatigue and excessive task complexity.
concepts.advanced: Working memory depends on dynamic frontoparietal coordination rather than a single storage site. Prefrontal systems support goal maintenance and interference control, while posterior regions represent domain-specific content. Capacity reflects both representational fidelity and the ability to protect task-relevant information from interference.
concepts.analogy: A small desk: if too many files are opened at once, important material gets buried or dropped.
concepts.care: Working-memory weaknesses affect multistep instructions, mental arithmetic, reading comprehension and self-regulation. External supports reduce load and often improve real-world functioning more than repeated “brain training.”
concepts.wrong: Severe new working-memory impairment with confusion, language change or neurological signs requires medical assessment. Anxiety, sleep loss and pain can also produce temporary reductions.
concepts.pearl: Reduce the load before concluding the person lacks the ability.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive mechanism map and references below for assessment implications and evidence sources.

quiz.question: Working memory is best described as:
options: Temporary maintenance and manipulation of information
Permanent storage of life events
Rapid visual scanning only
Automatic motor learning
quiz.explanation: Working memory keeps information active and available for current goals.

concepts.title: Episodic Memory Assessment
concepts.subtitle: Learning, storing and retrieving personally experienced information
concepts.simple: Episodic memory helps you remember events and information from a particular time and place. Learning, storing and retrieving are separate steps.
concepts.psych: Neuropsychological interpretation distinguishes encoding, consolidation, storage and retrieval. Learning slope, delayed retention, recognition, intrusion errors and cueing effects help identify where the process breaks down. Attention and executive organisation strongly affect initial learning.
concepts.advanced: The medial temporal system supports relational binding and consolidation, while prefrontal systems organise encoding and strategic retrieval. A rapid-forgetting pattern despite adequate learning may suggest storage dysfunction; improvement with cues may indicate retrieval inefficiency. These patterns are probabilistic and must be interpreted with base rates, effort and context.
concepts.analogy: A library system: encoding is cataloguing, storage is keeping the book, and retrieval is finding it later.
concepts.care: Different memory profiles imply different supports. Encoding problems benefit from simplification and repetition; retrieval problems benefit from cueing and structure; storage problems require stronger external compensation and medical investigation.
concepts.wrong: Rapidly progressive memory loss, disorientation, seizures or acute confusion requires medical assessment. Depression and anxiety may reduce efficiency without producing a classic amnestic syndrome.
concepts.pearl: Do not call every low delayed-recall score “memory loss”—first ask whether the information was learned adequately.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive mechanism map and references below for assessment implications and evidence sources.

quiz.question: Poor free recall that improves markedly with recognition most suggests:
options: Retrieval inefficiency
Complete storage failure
Normal vision
Motor slowing
quiz.explanation: Recognition support can reveal information that was stored but difficult to retrieve spontaneously.

concepts.title: Visuospatial Processing
concepts.subtitle: Perceiving where things are and how parts relate in space
concepts.simple: Visuospatial skills help you understand shapes, distance, direction and how pieces fit together. They are different from eyesight itself.
concepts.psych: Visuospatial performance draws on visual perception, spatial attention, construction, mental rotation and integration of parts into wholes. Dorsal-stream systems emphasise spatial action and location; ventral-stream systems emphasise object identity.
concepts.advanced: Right-lateralised parietal and occipitoparietal networks are prominent in spatial attention and construction, but performance is distributed and task-dependent. Errors may reflect neglect, simultanagnosia, apraxia, executive disorganisation, motor limitations or primary visual impairment. Qualitative error analysis is essential.
concepts.analogy: A navigation and blueprint system: one pathway identifies the object, another maps where it is and how to act in relation to it.
concepts.care: Psychologists must distinguish perceptual, attentional, motor and executive causes of poor construction. The same low score can arise from very different mechanisms and require different supports.
concepts.wrong: New visual-field loss, spatial neglect, severe disorientation or constructional decline after acute onset requires neurological assessment.
concepts.pearl: The drawing is not just a score—its error pattern is often the most clinically informative part.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive mechanism map and references below for assessment implications and evidence sources.

quiz.question: The dorsal visual stream is most associated with:
options: Spatial location and visually guided action
Word meaning
Autobiographical memory
Taste perception
quiz.explanation: The dorsal stream supports “where/how” processing.

concepts.title: Social Cognition in Neuropsychology
concepts.subtitle: Reading people, intentions, emotions and social context
concepts.simple: Social cognition is how the brain makes sense of other people. It helps us notice facial expressions, understand intentions, predict reactions and adjust our behaviour to the situation.
concepts.psych: Assessment usually samples emotion recognition, theory of mind, social inference, pragmatic communication and awareness of social norms. Performance depends on perception, language, executive control, autobiographical knowledge and cultural learning; a low score is not a direct measure of empathy or character.
concepts.advanced: Social cognition emerges from distributed systems including medial prefrontal cortex, temporoparietal junction, superior temporal sulcus, amygdala, insula and orbitofrontal regions. Tasks differ in perceptual, linguistic and executive load. Ecological validity is therefore central: structured test performance may not predict fast, ambiguous real-world interactions.
concepts.analogy: A social navigation system that combines facial signals, context, memory and predictions about other minds.
concepts.care: Psychologists use social-cognitive findings to understand interpersonal misunderstandings in autism, traumatic brain injury, frontotemporal dementia, psychosis and acquired neurological conditions. Interpretation should separate capacity from performance under stress, overload or unfamiliarity.
concepts.wrong: A sudden change in social judgement, disinhibition, emotional recognition or personality may indicate neurological or medical change and warrants appropriate assessment.
concepts.pearl: Do not turn a social-cognition score into a moral judgement. It describes task performance, not how much a person cares.

quiz.question: Which conclusion is most defensible after a low theory-of-mind score?
options: The person lacks empathy
The task indicates difficulty inferring mental states under those conditions
The person has autism
The person is intentionally rude
quiz.explanation: A low score supports a task-specific hypothesis and must be interpreted with language, executive load, culture and history.

concepts.title: Executive Function Assessment
concepts.subtitle: Testing goal management, inhibition, flexibility and self-monitoring
concepts.simple: Executive skills are the brain’s management tools. They help you start, plan, resist distractions, switch approach, monitor mistakes and finish what matters.
concepts.psych: Executive assessment samples inhibition, set shifting, planning, generativity, abstraction, monitoring and goal maintenance. No single test captures “executive function.” Scores are shaped by processing speed, language, motor output, motivation and task structure, so interpretation requires converging evidence.
concepts.advanced: Executive performance reflects dynamic frontoparietal, cingulo-opercular, salience and subcortical circuitry. Highly structured tests can reduce the very ambiguity that exposes executive difficulty in daily life. Process observations—rule loss, perseveration, impulsive starts, poor error correction and inefficient strategy—may be more informative than a composite score.
concepts.analogy: An air-traffic controller coordinating priorities, timing, switching and error correction rather than flying any one aircraft.
concepts.care: Executive findings guide supports for planning, initiation, inhibition and self-monitoring across ADHD, acquired brain injury, mood disorders and neurodegenerative conditions. Rating scales, collateral report and real-world tasks help address the test–life gap.
concepts.wrong: Rapidly emerging disorganisation, disinhibition, apathy or loss of judgement—especially with neurological signs—requires medical assessment rather than attribution to personality.
concepts.pearl: A person can perform adequately in a quiet, highly structured assessment and still have major executive disability in unstructured life.

quiz.question: Why should executive tests be interpreted as a battery rather than one score?
options: Executive function is a single skill
Each task mixes executive and non-executive demands
Norms are unnecessary
Only rating scales matter
quiz.explanation: Executive tasks combine control processes with speed, language, memory, perception and motor demands.

concepts.title: Language Assessment
concepts.subtitle: Mapping comprehension, expression, naming, repetition and discourse
concepts.simple: Language lets us understand and share meaning through words, sentences and conversation. A language problem can affect speaking, understanding, reading, writing or finding words.
concepts.psych: Neuropsychological language assessment examines auditory comprehension, naming, fluency, repetition, reading, writing and discourse. Performance must be interpreted in relation to hearing, speech-motor control, education, multilingual background and cultural-linguistic experience.
concepts.advanced: Contemporary models describe distributed dorsal and ventral language streams rather than isolated “centres.” Dorsal pathways support sound-to-articulation mapping and repetition; ventral pathways support sound-to-meaning mapping. Lesions, disconnection and network reorganisation produce variable aphasia profiles that rarely fit classical categories perfectly.
concepts.analogy: A communication network with linked systems for recognising sounds, accessing meaning, constructing messages and programming speech.
concepts.care: Precise description separates aphasia from dysarthria, apraxia of speech, memory failure, executive disorganisation and second-language effects. This distinction determines referral, rehabilitation targets and communication supports.
concepts.wrong: Sudden difficulty speaking, understanding, reading or writing is a stroke emergency until proven otherwise. Activate local emergency pathways immediately.
concepts.pearl: Word-finding difficulty is a symptom, not a diagnosis; inspect whether the breakdown is in perception, meaning, lexical access or speech production.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive mechanism map, quiz bank and references below to consolidate clinical interpretation.

quiz.question: Sudden aphasia should be treated as:
options: A personality issue
A stroke emergency until assessed
Normal ageing
Evidence of low intelligence
quiz.explanation: Acute language change is a time-critical neurological red flag.

concepts.title: Neuropsychological Case Formulation
concepts.subtitle: Integrating brain, behaviour, development and context into one testable account
concepts.simple: A case formulation is the best current explanation of why this person is having these difficulties now. It connects test results with history, health, environment and everyday function.
concepts.psych: Neuropsychological formulation integrates referral question, developmental and medical history, observed behaviour, cognitive profile, emotional state, functional impact and collateral data. It should compare competing hypotheses and explain both impairment and preserved abilities rather than reciting scores.
concepts.advanced: Good formulation is Bayesian and iterative: prior probability is updated by converging and disconfirming evidence. It separates aetiology from mechanism and functional consequence. Causal claims should be proportionate to data quality, base rates and test specificity, with explicit uncertainty and alternative explanations.
concepts.analogy: A detective’s working model that explains the evidence, identifies gaps and predicts what should be observed next.
concepts.care: Formulation translates assessment into decisions: diagnosis, medical referral, rehabilitation, educational support, risk management and treatment planning. It should be comprehensible to the client while preserving technical precision.
concepts.wrong: Do not attribute progressive decline, acute change or focal neurological signs to stress without appropriate medical investigation. Conversely, do not assume every cognitive complaint reflects structural brain disease.
concepts.pearl: The formulation is not the score summary. It is the reasoning that connects evidence to the referral question and recommendations.

quiz.question: What distinguishes formulation from score summary?
options: It lists more percentiles
It explains how evidence answers the referral question
It avoids uncertainty
It uses only test data
quiz.explanation: Formulation integrates evidence into a testable explanatory account.

concepts.title: Clinical Test Interpretation
concepts.subtitle: From standard scores to defensible clinical meaning
concepts.simple: A test score compares one performance with an appropriate reference group. Meaning comes from the whole pattern, the person’s background and what happened during testing—not from a number alone.
concepts.psych: Interpretation requires norm selection, reliability, confidence intervals, base rates, validity indicators and behavioural observations. Within-person scatter is common; statistically unusual differences are not automatically clinically meaningful. Conclusions should converge across tests, history and real-world function.
concepts.advanced: Observed scores contain true-score variance and measurement error. Multiple comparisons increase false-positive findings, while regression to the mean and imperfect reliability limit strong claims from isolated extremes. Premorbid estimates, demographic corrections and normative samples carry assumptions that require transparent evaluation.
concepts.analogy: Reading a weather map: one measurement matters, but the pattern, instrument accuracy and local conditions determine the forecast.
concepts.care: Responsible interpretation prevents overdiagnosis, missed impairment and false certainty. Reports should explain confidence, functional relevance and limitations in language clients and referrers can use.
concepts.wrong: Invalid or uninterpretable data should not be converted into confident diagnoses. Acute neurological red flags require medical action regardless of whether formal testing has been completed.
concepts.pearl: “Low” is not synonymous with “impaired,” and “average” is not synonymous with “unaffected.” Context determines clinical significance.
