quiz.question: A statistically rare score difference is automatically clinically significant.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Rarity is one consideration; reliability, base rates, history and functional impact determine clinical meaning.

concepts.title: Semantic Memory Assessment
concepts.subtitle: Knowledge, concepts and word meaning across the lifespan
concepts.simple: Semantic memory is your store of facts, concepts and word meanings—the knowledge you can use without remembering when or where you learned it.
concepts.psych: Assessment samples naming, vocabulary, category knowledge, word–picture matching and general information. Performance must be separated from language exposure, education, culture and sensory access.
concepts.advanced: Semantic knowledge depends on distributed modality-specific representations coordinated by anterior temporal hub regions. Degradation produces loss of conceptual specificity across tasks, whereas access problems may fluctuate with cueing and executive demand.
concepts.analogy: A living encyclopedia: episodic memory records the visit, while semantic memory stores what the place means.
concepts.care: Semantic profiles help distinguish developmental language differences, aphasia, semantic-variant primary progressive aphasia and broader dementia syndromes.
concepts.wrong: Progressive loss of word meaning, object knowledge or person recognition warrants neurological assessment, especially when everyday function is changing.
concepts.pearl: A naming error is not automatically a semantic-memory failure—inspect comprehension, cueing and consistency across modalities.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Which pattern most strongly suggests degraded semantic knowledge?
options: Naming improves fully with phonemic cues
The same concept is poorly understood across words and pictures
Recall is low only after distraction
Performance improves with repetition
quiz.explanation: The same concept is poorly understood across words and pictures is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Procedural Learning
concepts.subtitle: Skills, habits and learning through repeated action
concepts.simple: Procedural learning is how repeated practice turns an effortful action into a skill or habit.
concepts.psych: Procedural tasks assess gradual improvement across trials, often without requiring conscious recollection. Motor, perceptual and cognitive procedures rely on partly different circuits.
concepts.advanced: Corticostriatal and cerebellar systems support reinforcement, sequencing, prediction error and automatization. Dissociations between preserved skill learning and impaired episodic memory demonstrate that memory is not unitary.
concepts.analogy: Learning to ride a bicycle: the body can know how even when you cannot explain every movement.
concepts.care: Procedural learning may remain usable when explicit memory is weak, creating rehabilitation opportunities through repetition, environmental consistency and habit design.
concepts.wrong: New loss of previously automatic skills, gait change or motor sequencing difficulty requires assessment for neurological, movement or cerebellar disorders.
concepts.pearl: When explicit teaching fails, consistent practice in the real context may still build useful learning.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Which system is especially important for habit and procedural learning?
options: Medial temporal lobe alone
Corticostriatal circuits
Primary visual cortex alone
Broca area
quiz.explanation: Corticostriatal circuits is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Praxis and Apraxia
concepts.subtitle: Planning and performing learned purposeful actions
concepts.simple: Praxis is the ability to turn an idea for an action into the right sequence of movements. Apraxia is a breakdown in that process that is not explained by weakness alone.
concepts.psych: Assessment compares gesture to command, imitation, tool use and multistep action while controlling for comprehension, vision, sensation, weakness and coordination.
concepts.advanced: Praxis depends on left-lateralised parietofrontal networks, stored action representations and interhemispheric transfer. Ideomotor, conceptual and limb-kinetic patterns reflect different breakdowns but often overlap clinically.
concepts.analogy: A movement recipe: the muscles are available, but the plan or translation into action is disrupted.
concepts.care: Recognising apraxia changes rehabilitation, communication and safety planning because repeated verbal instruction alone may not solve a motor-planning problem.
concepts.wrong: Sudden apraxia may signal stroke; progressive apraxia can occur in neurodegenerative syndromes and requires neurological assessment.
concepts.pearl: Before diagnosing apraxia, prove that the person understood the command and had adequate strength, sensation and coordination.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: What must be excluded before concluding a gesture error reflects apraxia?
options: Only low mood
Weakness, comprehension and sensory limitations
Age alone
Hand preference only
quiz.explanation: Weakness, comprehension and sensory limitations is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Agnosia and Recognition
concepts.subtitle: Recognising objects, faces, sounds and meaning
concepts.simple: Recognition combines sensory details into an identity. Agnosia occurs when a person can sense something but cannot recognise what it is through that channel.
concepts.psych: Assessment distinguishes perceptual integration from access to stored meaning and tests recognition across visual, auditory and tactile modalities.
concepts.advanced: Occipitotemporal and modality-specific association networks transform sensory features into stable representations. Apperceptive patterns disrupt structural encoding; associative patterns disrupt linkage from an adequate percept to meaning.
concepts.analogy: A barcode scanner that can see the lines but either cannot assemble the code or cannot connect it to the product database.
concepts.care: The distinction between sensory loss, naming difficulty and recognition failure determines referral, environmental adaptation and rehabilitation.
concepts.wrong: Acute recognition failure, especially with visual-field loss or other focal signs, requires urgent neurological assessment.
concepts.pearl: Ask whether the person can match, copy, describe and recognise the same item through another sense.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: In associative visual agnosia, a person may be able to:
options: Neither see nor copy the object
Copy the object but not identify it
Recognise it normally in every modality
Only fail because of weakness
quiz.explanation: Copy the object but not identify it is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Hemispatial Neglect
concepts.subtitle: Failure to attend to one side of space
concepts.simple: Neglect is not blindness. The brain fails to prioritise information from one side of space, usually after injury to the opposite hemisphere.
concepts.psych: Assessment combines cancellation, line bisection, drawing, reading and functional observation because neglect varies by task, distance and reference frame.
concepts.advanced: Right-lateralised ventral attention and frontoparietal networks are commonly implicated. Neglect may be egocentric or allocentric and can affect personal, peripersonal or extrapersonal space.
concepts.analogy: A spotlight that persistently points to one side, leaving the other side outside awareness even though the eyes can receive it.
concepts.care: Neglect strongly affects falls, navigation, reading, dressing and rehabilitation engagement. Functional observation is essential because paper tasks can underestimate disability.
concepts.wrong: New neglect is a focal neurological emergency and should trigger urgent stroke assessment.
concepts.pearl: A normal visual field does not rule out neglect, and a field cut does not fully explain spatial inattention.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Which finding best differentiates neglect from primary visual loss?
options: Omission that changes with cueing and attentional task
Reduced acuity in both eyes
Weakness of one hand
Hearing loss
quiz.explanation: Omission that changes with cueing and attentional task is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Performance Validity
concepts.subtitle: Determining whether test performance is interpretable
concepts.simple: Performance-validity measures ask whether test results provide a dependable picture of current ability. They do not, by themselves, explain why performance was invalid.
concepts.psych: Interpretation uses multiple embedded and stand-alone indicators, behavioural consistency and context. Failure can reflect deliberate underperformance, misunderstanding, severe impairment, fatigue, pain, psychiatric symptoms or other factors.
concepts.advanced: Validity decisions require multivariate evidence, appropriate cut-offs and consideration of false-positive risk. A single failed indicator rarely justifies a categorical attribution of motive.
concepts.analogy: Checking whether a thermometer reading is trustworthy before diagnosing the weather.
concepts.care: Without valid engagement, cognitive scores may underestimate ability and should not be used for strong diagnostic or capacity conclusions.
concepts.wrong: Do not equate invalid performance with malingering. Intent is a separate forensic inference requiring broader evidence.
concepts.pearl: Validity is about the interpretability of data—not the moral character of the person.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: What does a failed performance-validity indicator establish by itself?
options: Deliberate deception
That the associated cognitive data may be uninterpretable
A specific diagnosis
Lack of disability
quiz.explanation: That the associated cognitive data may be uninterpretable is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Premorbid Ability Estimation
concepts.subtitle: Estimating functioning before illness or injury
concepts.simple: Premorbid estimation asks what a person’s abilities were probably like before a neurological illness or injury changed them.
concepts.psych: Methods combine demographic prediction, education and occupation, reading-based estimates, prior records and preserved abilities. Every method has assumptions and error.
concepts.advanced: Estimates are probabilistic and vulnerable to cultural, linguistic, educational and developmental bias. Reading tests may be invalid when language, dyslexia, aphasia or advanced dementia affect performance.
concepts.analogy: Reconstructing the original height of a building from plans, photographs and the parts still standing.
concepts.care: Change cannot be inferred from a low score without a defensible estimate of prior function. Overestimating baseline can falsely imply decline; underestimating it can miss meaningful loss.
concepts.wrong: Avoid demographic formulas or reading estimates when the normative assumptions do not fit the person.
concepts.pearl: Premorbid ability is an interval with uncertainty, not a single hidden true score.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Why should premorbid ability usually be expressed as a range?
options: Because norms are unnecessary
Because every estimate contains uncertainty and assumptions
Because cognitive decline cannot occur
Because reading is always preserved
quiz.explanation: Because every estimate contains uncertainty and assumptions is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Ecological Validity and Functional Cognition
concepts.subtitle: Connecting structured testing with everyday life
concepts.simple: Ecological validity asks whether test findings help explain what a person can actually do in daily life.
concepts.psych: Prediction improves when standard tests are combined with collateral report, observation, questionnaires, performance-based tasks and analysis of environmental demands.
concepts.advanced: The test–life gap reflects differences in structure, cueing, novelty, time pressure, multitasking and consequences. Functional cognition emerges from person–task–environment interaction, not cognition alone.
concepts.analogy: A driving simulator can reveal skills, but real traffic adds distraction, fatigue, weather and consequences.
concepts.care: Recommendations should target actual bottlenecks and environmental supports rather than assuming that a score maps directly onto independence.
concepts.wrong: Do not infer legal capacity, driving safety or independent living from one cognitive score without domain-specific functional evidence.
concepts.pearl: A structured clinic may conceal executive difficulty that appears when the person must organise themselves.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Why can a person perform well on executive tests but struggle at home?
options: Home never requires executive function
Tests provide structure and cues that daily life may not
Collateral report is always wrong
Scores measure motivation only
quiz.explanation: Tests provide structure and cues that daily life may not is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Psychiatric and State Effects on Cognition
concepts.subtitle: Interpreting cognition in the context of mood, anxiety, sleep, pain and medication
concepts.simple: Cognitive performance changes with the state of the whole person. Sleep loss, distress, pain and medication can slow or disrupt thinking without proving brain injury.
concepts.psych: Assessment considers symptom timing, effort, arousal, rumination, psychomotor change, medication effects, substance use and whether cognitive complaints match objective patterns.
concepts.advanced: State factors influence attention allocation, processing efficiency, reward sensitivity and encoding. They can coexist with neurological disorder, so interpretation should avoid false either–or reasoning.
concepts.analogy: A computer may run slowly because hardware is damaged, because too many programs are open, or both.
concepts.care: Integrating psychiatric and medical context prevents both psychologising neurological change and pathologising reversible state effects as permanent impairment.
concepts.wrong: Acute confusion, focal signs, seizures or rapid progression should never be attributed to anxiety or depression without medical assessment.
concepts.pearl: “Functional” and “organic” are not opposites; symptoms can arise from interacting brain, body and context mechanisms.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Which interpretation is most defensible?
options: Depression explains every low score
Neurological disease excludes state effects
Mood and neurological factors may both influence performance
Subjective complaints are meaningless
quiz.explanation: Mood and neurological factors may both influence performance is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Paediatric Neuropsychology
concepts.subtitle: Interpreting the developing brain in developmental context
concepts.simple: Children’s brains and skills are still developing, so assessment asks not only what a child can do now, but how their developmental pathway is unfolding.
concepts.psych: Interpretation integrates developmental history, learning opportunity, family and school context, adaptive function and uneven skill acquisition. Age norms do not replace developmental formulation.
concepts.advanced: Early injury can produce delayed-emerging deficits as later tasks demand undeveloped systems. Neurodevelopmental profiles are dynamic, and repeated assessment should balance monitoring value against practice effects and burden.
concepts.analogy: Assessing a house while it is still being built: some weaknesses appear only when the next storey is added.
concepts.care: Findings guide educational adjustments, caregiver support, rehabilitation and realistic expectations while protecting the child from deterministic labels.
concepts.wrong: Regression, seizures, acute behavioural change or loss of previously acquired skills requires medical and developmental investigation.
concepts.pearl: A normal score today does not guarantee that a vulnerable system will meet tomorrow’s developmental demands.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Why can effects of early brain injury emerge later?
options: Brain injury always resolves
Later developmental demands expose vulnerable systems
Norms become invalid at adolescence
Children cannot be assessed
quiz.explanation: Later developmental demands expose vulnerable systems is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Older-Adult Neuropsychology
concepts.subtitle: Separating healthy ageing, reversible factors and neurodegenerative change
concepts.simple: Ageing can make some thinking slower, but major loss of independence, rapid forgetting or progressive change is not automatically “normal ageing.”
concepts.psych: Assessment considers trajectory, daily function, sensory status, vascular risk, medication, mood, sleep and normative fit. Longitudinal change is often more informative than one isolated score.
concepts.advanced: Healthy ageing commonly affects processing speed and effortful retrieval while accumulated knowledge is relatively preserved. Neurodegenerative syndromes produce characteristic but overlapping network patterns; biomarker and medical data may be needed for aetiological diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: An older filing system may take longer to search, but losing the files themselves is a different problem.
concepts.care: Neuropsychology supports differential diagnosis, capacity decisions, care planning and compensatory strategies while avoiding both ageism and false reassurance.
concepts.wrong: Acute confusion suggests delirium; rapid progression, focal signs or marked functional decline requires prompt medical assessment.
concepts.pearl: Ask about change from the person’s own baseline, not whether they resemble an average older adult.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Which feature is least consistent with uncomplicated healthy ageing?
options: Slower processing speed
Occasional retrieval difficulty
Progressive loss of independent medication management
Benefit from cues
quiz.explanation: Progressive loss of independent medication management is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: Report Writing and Feedback
concepts.subtitle: Turning complex findings into accurate, useful and humane communication
concepts.simple: A good report explains what was found, what it means, what remains uncertain and what should happen next. Feedback helps the person understand and use that information.
concepts.psych: Reports should answer the referral question, integrate evidence, distinguish findings from inference, explain limitations and provide prioritised recommendations. Feedback should be collaborative, paced and adapted to comprehension and emotional response.
concepts.advanced: Communication is a clinical intervention. Excessive jargon, deterministic statements and unranked recommendations reduce uptake. Transparent uncertainty and strengths-based formulation improve accuracy without minimising impairment.
concepts.analogy: A map with a clear destination, hazards, confidence limits and practical routes—not a warehouse of raw measurements.
concepts.care: Accessible reporting supports informed decisions, treatment engagement, accommodations and therapeutic adjustment while reducing stigma and misunderstanding.
concepts.wrong: Avoid diagnostic claims beyond the evidence, copying generic recommendations and disclosing sensitive information without appropriate consent and governance.
concepts.pearl: The best recommendation is specific enough that someone knows what to do on Monday morning.
concepts.learnMore: Open the interactive clinical reasoning map, quiz bank and references below.

quiz.question: Which feature most improves a recommendation?
options: More technical jargon
A specific action linked to the identified mechanism
A longer test table
Avoiding uncertainty
quiz.explanation: A specific action linked to the identified mechanism is the best-supported answer.

concepts.title: What EEG Measures
concepts.subtitle: Scalp voltage reflects synchronised postsynaptic activity, not thoughts or single-neuron firing
concepts.simple: EEG primarily records voltage differences generated by aligned cortical pyramidal populations. The signal is strongest when many neurons change membrane potential together and their fields summate at the scalp.
concepts.psych: EEG offers millisecond temporal resolution but limited spatial specificity. It should be interpreted as a network-level physiological measure shaped by volume conduction, skull conductivity, geometry and reference choice.
concepts.advanced: EEG offers millisecond temporal resolution but limited spatial specificity. It should be interpreted as a network-level physiological measure shaped by volume conduction, skull conductivity, geometry and reference choice. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: A microphone outside a stadium: it captures the crowd’s coordinated roar better than one person’s voice.
concepts.care: EEG is useful for seizures, encephalopathy, sleep-related phenomena and state-dependent brain function, but it cannot independently diagnose most psychiatric conditions.
concepts.wrong: Over-interpreting scalp maps as direct pictures of deep-brain activity or personality can produce false certainty.
concepts.pearl: Always ask: what physiological generator, reference and artifact could plausibly create this pattern?

concepts.title: Cortical Generators
concepts.subtitle: Why pyramidal-cell geometry matters
concepts.simple: Parallel apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons form open fields whose postsynaptic currents can summate and propagate to the scalp.
concepts.psych: Radial and tangential dipoles project differently across electrode arrays. Deep, small or closed-field generators may be poorly visible despite clinically important activity.
concepts.advanced: Radial and tangential dipoles project differently across electrode arrays. Deep, small or closed-field generators may be poorly visible despite clinically important activity. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: Rows of tiny batteries aligned in the same direction create a measurable field; random orientations cancel.
concepts.care: Generator geometry explains why absence of a scalp EEG finding does not exclude focal pathology or seizures.
concepts.wrong: Assuming every cortical event is equally visible ignores orientation, depth and spatial extent.
concepts.pearl: Scalp EEG sensitivity is constrained by physics before interpretation even begins.

concepts.title: Volume Conduction
concepts.subtitle: How brain activity spreads through tissue to the scalp
concepts.simple: Electrical fields spread through cerebrospinal fluid, skull and skin before reaching electrodes. Each sensor therefore samples a mixture of sources.
concepts.psych: Volume conduction blurs spatial localisation and inflates zero-lag similarity between channels. Source modelling can reduce ambiguity but depends on modelling assumptions and signal quality.
concepts.advanced: Volume conduction blurs spatial localisation and inflates zero-lag similarity between channels. Source modelling can reduce ambiguity but depends on modelling assumptions and signal quality. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: Light shining through frosted glass spreads beyond its source.
concepts.care: This explains why topographic colour does not equal a sharply bounded cortical lesion and why connectivity metrics require caution.
concepts.wrong: Treating neighbouring electrodes as independent brain regions can exaggerate localisation and connectivity claims.
concepts.pearl: A scalp maximum is a clue to a field, not a GPS coordinate.

concepts.title: International 10–20 System
concepts.subtitle: Reproducible electrode placement using proportional head measurements
concepts.simple: The 10–20 system positions electrodes by percentages of nasion–inion and preauricular distances, creating consistent labels such as Fp1, Cz and O2.
concepts.psych: Standardised placement supports comparison across people and sessions. Extended 10–10 arrays increase spatial sampling but do not remove volume-conduction limits.
concepts.advanced: Standardised placement supports comparison across people and sessions. Extended 10–10 arrays increase spatial sampling but do not remove volume-conduction limits. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: A coordinate grid fitted to each person’s head rather than fixed centimetres.
concepts.care: Correct placement is foundational for lateralisation, topography, repeat testing and normative comparison.
concepts.wrong: Eyeballing electrode positions introduces systematic topographic error.
concepts.pearl: Bad coordinates cannot be repaired by sophisticated statistics.

concepts.title: Electrode Impedance
concepts.subtitle: Stable contact between electrode and scalp
concepts.simple: Impedance reflects opposition to current at the electrode–skin interface. High or markedly unequal impedance increases noise susceptibility and channel imbalance.
concepts.psych: Modern amplifiers tolerate higher absolute impedance than older systems, but low and reasonably balanced impedances remain important. Abrading aggressively can harm skin and is unnecessary.
concepts.advanced: Modern amplifiers tolerate higher absolute impedance than older systems, but low and reasonably balanced impedances remain important. Abrading aggressively can harm skin and is unnecessary. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: A loose audio cable crackles even when the music source is fine.
concepts.care: Checking impedance prevents avoidable artifact and improves confidence in subtle findings.
concepts.wrong: Chasing an arbitrary ultra-low number can damage skin; ignoring large channel differences can contaminate data.
concepts.pearl: Aim for safe, stable and balanced contact—not ritualistically perfect numbers.

concepts.title: References and Montages
concepts.subtitle: Every EEG trace is a voltage difference
concepts.simple: EEG channels display one electrode relative to another or to a calculated reference. Changing the montage changes the appearance, not the underlying recording.
concepts.psych: Bipolar, referential and average-reference montages answer different questions. Phase reversal, field distribution and common-reference contamination must be understood before localisation.
concepts.advanced: Bipolar, referential and average-reference montages answer different questions. Phase reversal, field distribution and common-reference contamination must be understood before localisation. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: The same landscape photographed from different viewpoints.
concepts.care: Montage switching is essential for distinguishing true fields from reference artifacts and for localising epileptiform activity.
concepts.wrong: Reading only one montage can hide or manufacture apparent abnormalities.
concepts.pearl: Never interpret a waveform without knowing what is being subtracted from what.

concepts.title: Sampling Rate and Aliasing
concepts.subtitle: Digitising EEG without losing or inventing frequencies
concepts.simple: Sampling converts continuous voltage into discrete time points. Frequencies above the Nyquist limit can fold into lower frequencies unless filtered before digitisation.
concepts.psych: Sampling rate should comfortably exceed twice the highest frequency of interest. Anti-alias filtering and transparent acquisition settings are mandatory for reproducibility.
concepts.advanced: Sampling rate should comfortably exceed twice the highest frequency of interest. Anti-alias filtering and transparent acquisition settings are mandatory for reproducibility. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: A spinning wheel filmed too slowly appears to rotate backwards.
concepts.care: Incorrect sampling can distort fast activity, muscle artifact and high-frequency oscillations.
concepts.wrong: Upsampling later cannot recover information that was never captured.
concepts.pearl: Acquisition choices define the ceiling of valid interpretation.

concepts.title: Filters and Time Constants
concepts.subtitle: Useful noise reduction with unavoidable trade-offs
concepts.simple: High-pass, low-pass and notch filters attenuate selected frequencies. They can clarify recordings but also distort amplitude, phase and waveform shape.
concepts.psych: Aggressive high-pass filtering can sharpen slow transients into false spikes; low-pass filtering can hide muscle or fast epileptiform activity. Raw data should remain available.
concepts.advanced: Aggressive high-pass filtering can sharpen slow transients into false spikes; low-pass filtering can hide muscle or fast epileptiform activity. Raw data should remain available. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: Photo editing that can reveal detail—or erase evidence.
concepts.care: Understanding filters prevents false positives and false negatives in routine and quantitative EEG.
concepts.wrong: Using filters to “make the EEG look normal” undermines interpretation.
concepts.pearl: A cleaner trace is not automatically a truer trace.

concepts.title: Amplitude Frequency and Phase
concepts.subtitle: Core dimensions of an oscillating signal
concepts.simple: Amplitude describes voltage size, frequency describes cycles per second, and phase describes position within a cycle.
concepts.psych: These features underpin visual EEG, spectral power and connectivity measures. They are mathematically separable but physiologically interdependent.
concepts.advanced: These features underpin visual EEG, spectral power and connectivity measures. They are mathematically separable but physiologically interdependent. Interpretation should remain conditional on recording state, montage, artifact burden, age, medication and the referral question; the method does not convert correlational signal features into a stand-alone diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: A pendulum can swing widely or narrowly, quickly or slowly, and start at different points in its cycle.

concepts.title: Thalamus Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Map the relay, association and regulatory nuclei linking cortex, subcortex and arousal systems
concepts.simple: The thalamus is a paired hub deep in the brain. Most sensory information, and many motor and attention signals, pass through specialised thalamic nuclei before reaching cortex.
concepts.psych: The thalamus is not a passive relay. Its nuclei gate information according to state, salience and cortical feedback, contributing to attention, arousal, memory and the coordination of distributed cognitive networks.
concepts.advanced: Each thalamus borders the third ventricle and is divided by internal medullary laminae into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups. Ventral posterior nuclei relay somatosensation; geniculate bodies relay visual and auditory information; ventral anterior and lateral nuclei participate in basal ganglia and cerebellar motor loops; anterior and mediodorsal nuclei support limbic and prefrontal functions; pulvinar and intralaminar nuclei contribute to association, attention and arousal. Clinical effects depend on laterality, vascular territory and network disconnection.
concepts.analogy: Think of a secure rail interchange: different platforms serve different destinations, while cortical feedback continually changes which trains are prioritised.
concepts.care: Thalamic injury can alter attention, memory, language, arousal, affect and sensory experience. Recognising a distributed thalamocortical pattern helps avoid mislabelling neurological changes as purely psychiatric.
concepts.wrong: A focal thalamic lesion may cause hemisensory loss, central pain, memory impairment, language or neglect-like symptoms, reduced alertness or executive change. Symptoms rarely identify a single nucleus without imaging and neurological examination.
concepts.pearl: Bilateral paramedian thalamic injury can produce profound arousal and memory disturbance because it disrupts midline nuclei and their widespread cortical connections.

concepts.simple: The hypothalamus is a small control region beneath the thalamus. It monitors the body and coordinates temperature, thirst, hunger, hormones, sleep timing, stress responses and autonomic activity.
concepts.psych: The hypothalamus translates internal bodily signals and context into endocrine, autonomic and motivated responses. It links interoception, emotion and behaviour through connections with the pituitary, brainstem, limbic system and cortex.
concepts.advanced: The hypothalamus forms the floor and inferolateral walls of the third ventricle. Its preoptic, anterior, tuberal and posterior regions contain nuclei with overlapping functions. The suprachiasmatic nucleus entrains circadian rhythms; paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei regulate neuroendocrine output; arcuate, lateral and ventromedial regions contribute to energy balance; mammillary bodies participate in memory circuitry; descending projections coordinate autonomic and defensive responses. Functional boundaries are networked rather than one-nucleus/one-function.
concepts.analogy: Think of it as the building-management system for the body: sensors report temperature, fuel, water and time, and the hypothalamus adjusts hormones, autonomic systems and behaviour to restore balance.
concepts.care: Sleep, appetite, stress reactivity, sexual behaviour, fatigue and autonomic symptoms can all involve hypothalamic systems. Understanding the circuitry improves biopsychosocial formulation without reducing symptoms to a single brain centre.
concepts.wrong: Lesions or dysfunction can disturb endocrine axes, circadian timing, temperature regulation, appetite, thirst, autonomic control and memory. Similar symptoms are common in non-hypothalamic conditions, so localisation requires medical assessment.
concepts.pearl: The hypothalamus is tiny but strategically placed: a small lesion can affect several endocrine, autonomic and behavioural systems at once.

quiz.question: Which hypothalamic nucleus is the principal circadian pacemaker?
options: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
Ventral lateral thalamus
Caudate nucleus
Red nucleus
quiz.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives retinal timing information and coordinates circadian rhythms.

concepts.title: Insula Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Map interoception, salience, taste and autonomic integration
concepts.simple: The insula is folded deep inside the lateral sulcus and helps integrate body signals with emotion, attention and action.
concepts.psych: The insula supports interoception, salience detection and switching between internally and externally focused networks.
concepts.advanced: The insular cortex contains posterior-to-anterior gradients from primary interoceptive and somatosensory representations toward multimodal, affective and cognitive integration. It connects with thalamus, amygdala, cingulate, orbitofrontal cortex, striatum and brainstem autonomic centres.
concepts.analogy: A concealed control room that combines body telemetry with context before signalling what deserves attention.
concepts.care: Insular dysfunction can contribute to altered interoception, disgust processing, craving, pain, panic and salience attribution, but symptoms reflect network-level dysfunction rather than a single-region diagnosis.
concepts.wrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt salience network, interoception, autonomic regulation; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
concepts.pearl: Do not equate strong bodily awareness or anxiety with an “overactive insula”; infer mechanisms cautiously.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the insula atlas?
options: The insula supports interoception, salience detection and switching between internally and externally focused networks.
It acts independently of the rest of the brain.
It has one fixed psychological function.
It can diagnose psychiatric disorders from anatomy alone.
quiz.rationale: The structure participates in distributed networks and should be interpreted in context.

concepts.title: Insula & Operculum Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Explore the buried insula and overlying frontal, parietal and temporal opercula
concepts.simple: The insula sits beneath cortical lids called opercula, which must be conceptually opened to see the buried cortex.
concepts.psych: The insula-operculum complex integrates interoception, taste, somatosensation, speech-motor coordination and salience.
concepts.advanced: The frontal, parietal and temporal opercula border the lateral sulcus and cover the insula. Their close spatial relationship explains why vascular lesions or epilepsy can produce mixed language, somatosensory, gustatory and autonomic symptoms.
concepts.analogy: A theatre stage hidden behind three curtains; opening each curtain reveals a different part of the same system.
concepts.care: This anatomy clarifies why lateral perisylvian lesions can create blended cognitive, sensory and motor presentations.
concepts.wrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt speech motor planning, gustation, interoception; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
concepts.pearl: When symptoms cross taste, speech, face sensation and autonomic state, think regionally rather than forcing a single-lobe explanation.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the insula & operculum atlas?
options: The insula-operculum complex integrates interoception, taste, somatosensation, speech-motor coordination and salience.
It acts independently of the rest of the brain.
It has one fixed psychological function.
It can diagnose psychiatric disorders from anatomy alone.
quiz.rationale: The structure participates in distributed networks and should be interpreted in context.

concepts.title: Cingulate Cortex Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Trace anterior, midcingulate and posterior cingulate functions
concepts.simple: The cingulate cortex curves around the corpus callosum and helps connect motivation, pain, attention, memory and emotion.
concepts.psych: Different cingulate zones participate in salience, action selection, autonomic regulation, error monitoring and internally directed cognition.
concepts.advanced: Anterior and midcingulate sectors connect strongly with prefrontal, insular, limbic, motor and autonomic systems; posterior cingulate and retrosplenial regions are central nodes in memory and default-mode networks. Boundaries are functional gradients rather than rigid boxes.
concepts.analogy: A bridge running around the brain’s central highway, linking body state, motivation, action and memory.
concepts.care: Cingulate lesions may alter initiation, error monitoring, affect, pain experience, memory orientation or self-referential processing depending on location and connectivity.
concepts.wrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt salience network, default mode network, pain matrix; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
concepts.pearl: “Cingulate dysfunction” is too broad to be clinically useful—specify the subregion, network and task demand.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the cingulate cortex atlas?
options: Different cingulate zones participate in salience, action selection, autonomic regulation, error monitoring and internally directed cognition.
It acts independently of the rest of the brain.
It has one fixed psychological function.
It can diagnose psychiatric disorders from anatomy alone.
quiz.rationale: The structure participates in distributed networks and should be interpreted in context.

concepts.title: Reticular Activating System Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Map ascending arousal pathways from brainstem to thalamus and cortex
concepts.simple: The reticular activating system helps keep the brain awake, alert and responsive.
concepts.psych: Arousal depends on distributed brainstem, hypothalamic, basal forebrain, thalamic and cortical systems rather than one switch.
concepts.advanced: Ascending neuromodulatory nuclei include noradrenergic locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe, cholinergic pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, dopaminergic midbrain systems and histaminergic tuberomammillary pathways. These converge through thalamic and extrathalamic routes to regulate cortical state.
concepts.analogy: A building-wide power and alertness network with several backup generators, not a single light switch.
concepts.care: Damage can produce reduced consciousness, fluctuating attention, sleep-wake disruption or impaired state regulation; diffuse metabolic and pharmacological effects can mimic focal disruption.
concepts.wrong: Damage or dysregulation can disrupt arousal, sleep-wake regulation, attention readiness; presentations depend on laterality, extent and connected networks.
concepts.pearl: Always separate arousal level from cognitive content: a person cannot demonstrate cognition reliably when state regulation is unstable.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the reticular activating system atlas?
options: Arousal depends on distributed brainstem, hypothalamic, basal forebrain, thalamic and cortical systems rather than one switch.
It acts independently of the rest of the brain.
It has one fixed psychological function.
It can diagnose psychiatric disorders from anatomy alone.
quiz.rationale: The structure participates in distributed networks and should be interpreted in context.

concepts.title: Pituitary Gland & Sella Turcica Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Explore pituitary compartments, sellar relationships and hypothalamic control
concepts.simple: The pituitary is a pea-sized hormone gland in a bony pocket beneath the brain. It receives instructions from the hypothalamus and helps regulate growth, stress, reproduction, thyroid function, water balance and lactation.
concepts.psych: The pituitary is a major endocrine interface between brain and body. Changes in pituitary or hypothalamic function can alter energy, sleep, mood, cognition, sexual function, appetite and stress physiology, but these symptoms are nonspecific and require medical assessment.
concepts.advanced: The hypophysis sits in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone. The anterior lobe receives hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting factors through the superior hypophyseal portal circulation; the posterior lobe contains axon terminals from supraoptic and paraventricular hypothalamic neurons. Superiorly lie the diaphragma sellae, infundibulum and optic chiasm; laterally are the cavernous sinuses containing the internal carotid arteries and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI; inferiorly lies the sphenoid sinus. Sellar and parasellar lesions may therefore combine endocrine, visual-field, ocular-motor, facial sensory and headache presentations.
concepts.analogy: Think of the hypothalamus as the executive office and the pituitary as the dispatch centre. The sella is the reinforced control booth, but nearby visual and cranial-nerve cables make expansion clinically important.
concepts.care: Pituitary disease can mimic or amplify depression, anxiety, fatigue, cognitive slowing, irritability, sleep disturbance and changes in motivation. Psychologists should recognise red flags and avoid assuming that endocrine-linked symptoms are purely psychological.
concepts.wrong: Pituitary hormone excess or deficiency can produce broad systemic and neuropsychiatric effects. Expanding masses may compress the optic chiasm, invade the cavernous sinus or disturb hypothalamic pathways. Symptom patterns vary with hormone type, lesion size, growth direction, treatment and comorbidity.
concepts.pearl: A combination of new visual-field change, persistent headache and endocrine symptoms is a sellar-region red flag, not a personality formulation.

quiz.question: Which structure is most vulnerable to a pituitary mass expanding superiorly?
options: Optic chiasm
Cerebellar vermis
Medial lemniscus
Primary auditory cortex
quiz.explanation: The optic chiasm lies immediately superior to the sella, so superior expansion can disturb crossing visual fibres.

concepts.title: Basal Ganglia Circuit Explorer
concepts.subtitle: Trace direct, indirect and hyperdirect loops through cortex, striatum, pallidum, subthalamic nucleus and thalamus
concepts.simple: Trace direct, indirect and hyperdirect loops through cortex, striatum, pallidum, subthalamic nucleus and thalamus.
concepts.psych: Frontostriatal loops influence motivation, reinforcement learning, response inhibition and cognitive flexibility; abnormalities are transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific.
concepts.advanced: Location: Deep bilateral nuclei surrounding the internal capsule, linked with frontal cortex, thalamus and midbrain. Major subdivisions include caudate nucleus, putamen, nucleus accumbens, globus pallidus external, globus pallidus internal, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra pars compacta, substantia nigra pars reticulata, motor thalamus. Inputs include frontal cortex, sensorimotor cortex, limbic cortex, substantia nigra pars compacta; outputs include motor thalamus, brainstem motor regions, frontal cortex via thalamus.
concepts.analogy: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
concepts.care: Frontostriatal loops influence motivation, reinforcement learning, response inhibition and cognitive flexibility; abnormalities are transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific.
concepts.wrong: Disruption may contribute to hypokinetic or hyperkinetic movement, impaired initiation, altered habit learning, impulsivity or apathy. Clinical expression depends on circuit, laterality, cause and network compensation.
concepts.pearl: Do not reduce the basal ganglia to “movement centres”: specify the motor, associative or limbic loop and the direction of circuit imbalance.

quiz.question: Which pathway provides a rapid cortical route to increase inhibitory basal-ganglia output?
options: Hyperdirect pathway
Direct pathway
Dorsal column pathway
Medial forebrain bundle
quiz.rationale: The hyperdirect pathway projects from cortex to subthalamic nucleus, rapidly increasing GPi/SNr output and suppressing competing actions.

concepts.title: Major White-Matter Pathways Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Explore projection, association, commissural and limbic fibre systems
concepts.simple: Explore projection, association, commissural and limbic fibre systems.
concepts.psych: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.
concepts.advanced: Location: Distributed myelinated fibre bundles connecting cortical, subcortical, brainstem and spinal regions across both hemispheres. Major subdivisions include corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus, arcuate fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, cingulum bundle, fornix, optic radiations, corticospinal tract. Inputs include cortical neurons, thalamic nuclei, hippocampal formation, brainstem nuclei; outputs include contralateral cortex, ipsilateral cortical targets, subcortical nuclei, brainstem and spinal cord.
concepts.analogy: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
concepts.care: White-matter integrity constrains processing speed, executive coordination and network synchronisation, but imaging associations are probabilistic and influenced by age, vascular health and methodology.
concepts.wrong: Disconnection may produce weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, neglect, visual-field deficits, amnesia or slowed processing depending on tract and network. Diffuse disease often causes broad inefficiency rather than a single focal syndrome.
concepts.pearl: When grey matter looks intact but function is not, ask whether the pathway between nodes has failed.

quiz.question: Which fibre class connects the two cerebral hemispheres?
options: Commissural fibres
Projection fibres only
Peripheral nerves
Spinothalamic fibres
quiz.rationale: Commissural pathways, especially the corpus callosum, connect homologous and heterologous regions across hemispheres.

concepts.title: Neurotransmitter Pathways Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Trace major monoaminergic, cholinergic and amino-acid signalling systems
concepts.simple: Trace major monoaminergic, cholinergic and amino-acid signalling systems.
concepts.psych: Neurotransmitters modulate distributed circuits. Terms such as “chemical imbalance” are clinically misleading when used as simple explanations for complex mental disorders.
concepts.advanced: Location: Small brainstem, midbrain, hypothalamic and basal-forebrain nuclei project broadly, while glutamate and GABA operate throughout local and long-range circuits. Major subdivisions include locus coeruleus, dorsal and median raphe, ventral tegmental area, substantia nigra pars compacta, basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei, tuberomammillary nucleus, cortical glutamate systems, GABA interneuron networks. Inputs include prefrontal cortex, hypothalamus, brainstem sensory systems, limbic structures; outputs include cerebral cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, spinal and autonomic systems.
concepts.analogy: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
concepts.care: Neurotransmitters modulate distributed circuits. Terms such as “chemical imbalance” are clinically misleading when used as simple explanations for complex mental disorders.
concepts.wrong: Focal or degenerative disruption may alter arousal, movement, memory, autonomic regulation or affect, but behavioural effects emerge from receptor distribution and network state rather than transmitter level alone.
concepts.pearl: A neurotransmitter is not an emotion: it changes the gain and plasticity of circuits that generate behaviour in context.

quiz.question: Which nucleus is the major source of cortical noradrenergic projections?
options: Locus coeruleus
Caudate nucleus
Mammillary body
Red nucleus
quiz.rationale: The locus coeruleus provides widespread noradrenergic innervation to cortex and many subcortical regions.

concepts.title: Functional Network Overlay Atlas
concepts.subtitle: Overlay default-mode, salience, executive, dorsal-attention and sensorimotor systems
concepts.simple: Overlay default-mode, salience, executive, dorsal-attention and sensorimotor systems.
concepts.psych: Network models fit transdiagnostic formulation better than single-region explanations, but resting-state correlations are not direct measures of thoughts or diagnoses.
concepts.advanced: Location: Large-scale networks span noncontiguous cortical and subcortical nodes, often overlapping within hub regions. Major subdivisions include default mode network, salience network, frontoparietal control network, dorsal attention network, ventral attention network, sensorimotor network, visual network, limbic network. Inputs include sensory systems, interoceptive signals, memory systems, task goals, reward and threat signals; outputs include motor systems, autonomic systems, memory updating, attention allocation, goal-directed behaviour.
concepts.analogy: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
concepts.care: Network models fit transdiagnostic formulation better than single-region explanations, but resting-state correlations are not direct measures of thoughts or diagnoses.
concepts.wrong: Damage or dysconnectivity may disturb attention, self-related thought, executive control, awareness or behaviour. Similar symptoms can arise from different nodes, and one lesion can affect several networks.
concepts.pearl: Ask which network should dominate for the task, which network should disengage, and whether switching between them is efficient.

quiz.question: Which network is most associated with detecting behaviourally relevant internal and external events and coordinating switching?
options: Salience network
Primary visual network
Corticospinal tract
Dorsal column system
quiz.rationale: The salience network, particularly anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate regions, is implicated in relevance detection and network switching.

concepts.title: Arterial Territories & Stroke Comparison
concepts.subtitle: Compare ACA, MCA, PCA, perforator and posterior-circulation lesion patterns
concepts.simple: Compare ACA, MCA, PCA, perforator and posterior-circulation lesion patterns.
concepts.psych: Post-stroke mood, fatigue, apathy and cognitive change reflect lesion location, network disconnection, systemic illness, disability and psychosocial context rather than a single “stroke personality.”
concepts.advanced: Location: Arterial territories cover cortical surfaces, deep nuclei, white matter, brainstem and cerebellum with substantial anatomical variation and collateral overlap. Major subdivisions include anterior cerebral artery territory, middle cerebral artery territory, posterior cerebral artery territory, lenticulostriate arteries, anterior choroidal artery, posterior inferior cerebellar artery, anterior inferior cerebellar artery, superior cerebellar artery, basilar perforators. Inputs include internal carotid circulation, vertebrobasilar circulation, circle of Willis collateral routes; outputs include cortical branches, deep perforators, brainstem and cerebellar branches.
concepts.analogy: A dynamic transport and control map: the meaning of any node depends on the routes entering, leaving and bypassing it.
concepts.care: Post-stroke mood, fatigue, apathy and cognitive change reflect lesion location, network disconnection, systemic illness, disability and psychosocial context rather than a single “stroke personality.”
concepts.wrong: Ischaemia or haemorrhage may produce contralateral motor/sensory deficits, aphasia, neglect, visual-field loss, memory disturbance, ataxia, cranial-nerve findings or altered consciousness depending on site and extent.
concepts.pearl: Time plus territory matters: sudden focal deficit is vascular until proven otherwise, and urgent stroke pathways outrank elegant localisation.

quiz.question: A dominant-hemisphere superior-division MCA stroke most classically threatens:
options: Expressive language and face-arm motor systems
Only leg sensation
Bilateral hearing exclusively
Pituitary hormone release
quiz.rationale: The dominant lateral frontal territory includes language-production and face-arm motor regions, though actual patterns vary.

concepts.title: Brain Lateralisation Comparison
concepts.subtitle: Compare hemispheric specialisation without reducing people to left-brain or right-brain types
concepts.simple: The hemispheres work as a connected pair. Some operations are weighted more strongly to one side, but neither hemisphere is a complete personality or a self-sufficient thinking style.
concepts.psych: Language is commonly left-lateralised, whereas right-lateralised networks often contribute strongly to broad spatial attention, emotional prosody and discourse context. These are population tendencies within bilateral systems, not personality categories or stand-alone diagnostic markers.
concepts.advanced: Hemispheric specialisation emerges from asymmetries in cortical organisation, intrahemispheric connectivity and interhemispheric coordination. Lesion effects depend on cortical and subcortical extent, white-matter disconnection, vascular territory, premorbid organisation, diaschisis and recovery.
concepts.analogy: A skilled two-person team: each member may take the lead for particular operations, but useful performance depends on continuous exchange and shared context.
concepts.care: Laterality helps formulate aphasia, neglect, aprosodia, awareness, memory and executive presentations. It should guide testable hypotheses, not be used to infer creativity, logic, personality or diagnosis from preferences or handedness.
concepts.wrong: Dominant perisylvian injury may impair language; right frontoparietal injury may produce left neglect or impaired awareness; right perisylvian injury may alter affective prosody; callosal injury may cause task-specific disconnection signs. Real presentations frequently overlap or depart from textbook patterns.
concepts.pearl: Ask which network, pathway and side are affected—and what the person could do before the lesion—rather than asking whether someone is left-brained or right-brained.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes hemispheric lateralisation?
options: Relative specialisation within strongly connected bilateral systems
Separate logical and creative personality types
Complete independence of the two hemispheres
A fixed trait determined only by handedness
quiz.rationale: Lateralisation describes relative functional weighting; most complex behaviour depends on bilateral networks and interhemispheric exchange.

concepts.title: Healthy Versus Pathology Comparison
concepts.subtitle: Compare variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder without treating a scan as a diagnosis
concepts.simple: Healthy brains vary. A scan difference may be harmless, while important dysfunction may occur without a visible structural lesion.
concepts.psych: Variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder overlap but are not interchangeable. Interpretation requires clinical context, impairment, time course and converging evidence.
concepts.advanced: Structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative patterns have different meanings. Network disconnection, diaschisis, compensation, reserve and comorbidity shape phenotype, and imaging alone does not establish diagnosis.
concepts.analogy: A city map and a traffic report describe different aspects of the same system; neither alone explains how one resident is functioning.
concepts.care: Careful framing prevents biological essentialism, false reassurance from an unremarkable scan and overdiagnosis from incidental findings.
concepts.wrong: Similar symptoms can arise through different mechanisms, and similar biological findings can have different functional consequences.
concepts.pearl: Ask whether the finding, time course, network and examination converge before attributing a symptom or diagnosis.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes an imaging finding from a diagnosis?
options: A finding becomes diagnostic only when appropriately combined with clinical and other evidence
Any visible difference proves disorder
An unremarkable scan excludes dysfunction
Functional imaging independently establishes psychiatric diagnosis
quiz.rationale: Imaging is one evidence source; diagnosis depends on validated criteria and convergence with phenotype, course and examination.

concepts.title: Lesion and Symptom Mapping
concepts.subtitle: Relate lesions to pathways, networks, laterality, vascular territories and qualified symptom patterns
concepts.simple: A lesion affects tissue at one place, but symptoms depend on the pathways, networks and context around it. The map supports hypotheses, not certainty.
concepts.psych: Cognition, emotion and behaviour emerge from distributed systems. Laterality, disconnection, diaschisis, reserve, development and time since injury all shape presentation.
concepts.advanced: Lesion-symptom inference combines topography and mechanism with tract anatomy, network membership, hemispheric specialisation, vascular territory and temporal evolution. Many-to-many mapping is expected.
concepts.analogy: A rail fault may damage one station, sever a track between intact stations or destabilise the timetable across the network.
concepts.care: Qualified mapping guides assessment and rehabilitation while preventing biological overclaiming and one-region-one-symptom conclusions.
concepts.wrong: Focal lesions, disconnections and distributed network dysfunction can produce overlapping patterns, while similar lesions can have different consequences.
concepts.pearl: Ask what is focal, what is disconnected, what is distributed and which alternatives could produce the same findings.

quiz.question: Why is one-lesion-one-symptom reasoning unsafe?
options: Symptoms and lesions have many-to-many relationships shaped by pathways, networks and individual context
Every symptom has one necessary cortical centre
Laterality does not influence function
Only lesion volume matters
quiz.rationale: A lesion can disturb several connected functions, while the same symptom can arise from different nodes, tracts or physiological mechanisms.

concepts.title: Integrated Whole-Brain Explorer and Capstone
concepts.subtitle: Integrate and navigate the complete Interactive Anatomy atlas from one whole-brain entry point
concepts.simple: The brain works as one connected system. Choose a domain, add an overlay and open any completed detailed anatomy structure.
concepts.psych: Cognition, emotion and behaviour depend on cortical, subcortical, cerebellar and brainstem interactions linked by fibres, networks and vascular supply.
concepts.advanced: Integrated localisation combines tissue compartment, laterality, tract course, network topology, vascular distribution, lesion mechanism and temporal context.
concepts.analogy: A city map can layer neighbourhoods, rail lines, utilities, traffic zones and disruptions on one shared base.
concepts.care: The capstone links clinical findings to plausible systems while preserving differential diagnosis, reserve, development and psychosocial context.
concepts.wrong: Focal injury can disconnect pathways and alter remote nodes; distributed disease can cross structures, territories and networks.
concepts.pearl: Ask where, which fibres, which networks, which mechanism and what evidence could disconfirm the hypothesis.

quiz.question: What is the best first step when using the integrated explorer for a new clinical pattern?
options: Orient to the whole-brain pattern and time course before narrowing by laterality, pathway, network and mechanism
Choose the single region most associated with one symptom
Assume the largest overlay is causal
Ignore normal variation
quiz.rationale: Broad orientation prevents premature localisation and supports structured comparison of sites, pathways, networks and mechanisms.
